#2774. Caleb Williams: I could throw 100 picks and I wouldn't get gun-shy

Bears quarterback Caleb Williams threw four interceptions on Sunday night against the Buccaneers, but he wasn’t hesitant to keep throwing downfield at the end of the game, when he led the Bears into range for the game-winning field goal.

Williams hit a wide-open Colston Loveland for a 38-yard gain in the final minute of the game to set up a field goal as time expired on the Bears’ 27-24 win, and Williams said there was no hesitation to pull the trigger, despite his four interceptions. And he said he would have had no hesitation to pull the trigger even if Loveland hadn’t been wide open.

“I’m gonna throw until I can’t throw anymore. That’s how I live,” Williams said. “I work my tail off to be in this position. I’ll never not throw the ball. I could throw 100 picks in one game, if it comes down to it I’m gonna throw that pass that I threw to Colston, or if it’s a tighter window I’m gonna rip it in there. That’s how I grew up, that’s what I am. I don’t get gun-shy. That’s not me. That’s not my identity, not who I am. I’m gonna keep ripping it, keep ripping it.”

Williams admitted that he needs to find ways to get better, especially when the defense is blitzing him, but after the game he didn’t sound particularly concerned about the four interceptions. He’ll keep throwing confidently no matter how many get intercepted.

#2773. How Hawkins overcame illness to star for England

When Rob Hawkins replied to what he thought was an advert to play wheelchair basketball more than a decade ago he could not have imagined he would be a key part of an England side defending their Rugby League World Cup title.

While the men's and women's teams have already returned home, England face Australia in Wollongong on Tuesday (08:45 GMT) in the semi-finals of the Wheelchair competition, aiming to take another step towards becoming the first nation to lift the trophy on three occasions.

However, 25-year-old Hawkins, who was a big presence in the side to triumph in Manchester four years ago, has also had to overcome the odds - and a battle with chronic fatigue syndrome - to become one of the stars of the international game.

The England and Halifax Panthers wing only took up rugby league in 2014 after being bedbound for 18 months, and following a quirk of fate.

"Before my condition I was very sporting and athletic. I'd been doing running, football, started getting into other sports like rugby league and so I wanted to try and find something that interested me," Hawkins told BBC Sport.

"I saw something on television about wheelchair basketball so we tried looking for our local club, and what we thought was Halifax wheelchair basketball. When we went to a session it turned out it was wheelchair rugby league instead.

"I thought I'd give it a try and see what I thought. I jumped into a chair for about 20 minutes before my body probably wouldn't let me continue any more and I just kept wanting to go back and get better. It was definitely an interesting turn of events but I don't regret any minute of staying in the sport.

"When I found out that I could play internationally it kind of drove my competitiveness back out that I didn't have since before the condition."

Hawkins won the coveted IRL Golden Boot Award in 2024 and 2025 after being voted the International Wheelchair Player of the Year.

He is also Super League's reigning Wheels of Steel winner, given to the best player in the competition.

Yet it did not always come so easy. His condition previously meant that he had to use walking frames or rely on family members just to get to the toilet, and he also missed two years of learning at high school.

"There are still times where I just need that extra rest," he added.

"There are days where I still go down and I do just rest all day long. The thing that I've just learned over the years is effectively just trying to pace myself as much as I can.

"It feels weird to say - I'm happy I've had this condition because it's taught me and seemed to show me a different aspect of life where I've actually connected with people that I might not have done previously."

USA NS Pacific Islands to host 2030 World Cup

The England team who can still win the Rugby League World Cup

England go into their semi-final against hosts Australia as favourites to reach the showpiece match.

They followed a 98-18 victory over Wales with a 134-0 win against the USA before defeating Ireland 68-32 to top Pool A.

Australia claimed thumping wins over New Zealand and Scotland before their momentum was checked by a 69-34 loss to France, who were runners-up four years ago.

However, having pushed England close in the 2025 Ashes, Hawkins says that while England will not underestimate their opponents, they are relishing the challenge in front of them.

"I'm excited for the pressure," Hawkins added.

"We know they have been bringing a decent crowd in and that it is going to be a difficult game with the atmosphere and with the team that we're facing, but we also know that we are confident to basically go and do our game and stick to our game plan as well.

"We have some ladders in our team room and every game that we've won so far we've been spray painting it gold.

"We're just taking that one step up the ladder every time - we're just looking forward to facing Australia."

#2771. Joe Mazzulla spoke with Kristaps Porziņģis after his decision to step away from basketball

Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla had a heartfelt conversation with Kristaps Porziņģis on the team's flight to Milwaukee. Their chat left Mazzulla with plenty to reflect on, and he shared those thoughts before Sunday night's game against the Bucks.

"I talked to him on the plane. I reached out to him," Mazzulla told reporters pregame, per CLNS Media. "I had a good conversation with him. Also, some of my other guys on the staff did as well. I think it's just a good reminder of what we go through in an NBA season. When you look at these guys as athletes and as basketball players, they're a lot more than that."

HOUSTON, TEXAS – JANUARY 03: Kristaps Porzingis #8 of the Boston Celtics speaks with head coach Joe Mazzulla during the second half against the Houston Rockets at Toyota Center on January 03, 2025 in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images

On Friday, Porziņģis announced he would "step away" from basketball to focus on his health as he continues battling postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), a condition that has sidelined him since the start of the season. Porziņģis' symptoms first emerged during his final season with the Celtics in February 2025, and continued lingering during his follow-up stints with the Atlanta Hawks and Golden State Warriors.

Porziņģis signed a two-year, $40 million deal with Golden State this past summer, making the 31-year-old's search for a "solution," as he described it, all the more pressing.

His 57-game debut season with the Celtics, which culminated in the 2024 NBA championship, was the last time we saw Porziņģis in his 'unicorn' form. Acquired via trade with the Wizards in exchange for Marcus Smart, Porziņģis needed little time to win over the Boston crowd. He averaged 20.1 points and 7.2 rebounds per game before delivering an electric performance in Game 1 of the NBA Finals against the Mavericks, scoring 20 points, grabbing six rebounds and recording three blocks in just 21 minutes.

He left Boston a champion and cemented his Celtics legacy, although Mazzulla wasn't focused on any of that.

Instead, Mazzulla opened up about his broader perspective, stressing the importance of connecting with the person behind the jersey rather than simply the player. With health concerns reminding everyone — including professional athletes — that there's more to life than basketball, Mazzulla values the moments he shares with his players away from the court just as much as their accomplishments on it.

"Their platforms, their life, their careers are so much more than what happens on the court," Mazzulla said. "So it's a good reminder of that. We're able to talk to him about it, but he's in a pretty good space. Whatever we can do to help him, we will. And I'm grateful for the time I got to spend with him on and off the court."

The pressure was immediate when Porziņģis arrived in Boston. Not only had the organization parted ways with Smart, a beloved fan favorite, to bring him aboard, but the expectations were immediately championship-or-bust as he joined forces with Jayson Tatum, Jaylen Brown, Al Horford, and Jrue Holiday to form an all-time great Celtics roster.

Boston, MA – April 23 – Kristaps Porzingis #8 of the Boston Celtics smiles after getting hit in the head during the third quarter of Game 2 of the Eastern Conference Finals at the TD Garden. (Photo by Matt Stone/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images

Porziņģis seamlessly connected with both the fanbase and his new teammates. He even lived in the same apartment building as Brown, as the two would frequently carpool to games and sit side-by-side on flights together.

"Just a guy, when he comes into a room, he lights the room up, lights the locker room up," Mazzulla said. "I thought the years he was [in Boston], he was like the icebreaker. He brought a sense of joy to the rigors of the season and playing for the Celtics, and he brought a joy to that. I think he had a positive impact on the locker room."

For everything Porziņģis accomplished in Boston before his time with the Celtics came to an end, Mazzulla remains grateful. But he's also mindful. He understands that Banner 18, the performances and the unforgettable moments that will forever live in the organization's history, represent only part of what Porziņģis meant to him and the team. Their relationship extends well beyond basketball — something Mazzulla made clear.

#2770. Chris Jones: I lied when I said sacks don't matter, sacks are everything

The Chiefs came into Sunday’s game against the Jets with nine sacks on the season and that didn’t stop them from winning five of their first seven games, but it did lead to a lot of questions about whether the pass rush would come to life.

Defensive tackle Chris Jones responded to those questions after Week 8 by saying that sacks are overrated and that stats can sometimes be deceptive in regard to how the unit is performing across the board. Jones had a different answer after Sunday’s 35-12 win over the Jets.

The Chiefs had five sacks in the game and Jones had two of them after managing just a half-sack in the team’s first seven contests. That led him to change his tune about their value in the postgame press conference.

“Listen, I know last week, I was like, ‘Sacks don’t matter,’” Jones said. “I lied. Sacks are everything.”

The Chiefs will take wins any way they get them, but Sunday was a good example of how sacks can pile up when you’re playing from in front. They had one sack while building a 14-12 halftime lead and then teed off on Geno Smith once they were able to force the Jets into passing mode more often. The Chiefs tend toward closer shaves and going the opposite way on Sunday paid off for Jones and the entire defensive front.

#2768. Commanders had one final shot at the end zone, and they blew it

The Commanders, in key moments of games, continue to have a little too much Backward Hat Energy.

On Sunday, it wasn’t an issue of letting the clock expire or not knowing it was fourth down. Which made it less obvious on the surface.

Still, Commanders coach Dan Quinn made another questionable (to put it kindly) decision at the conclusion of the 20-13 loss to the Rams.

Fast forward through 59 minutes and 57 seconds. Three seconds remained. The Commanders had the ball on the L.A. 31.

The Commanders dialed up a goofy, clunky, Stanford band play. It went more like Benny Hill.

They were at the 31. Throw it to the end zone. Not a Hail Mary. A normal throw.

Remember the touchdown pass that Jayden Daniels threw to cap the Monday night game at Cincinnati in the third week of his rookie season? That was from 27 yards.

Sure, the Bengals weren’t guarding the end zone; the Rams would have been.

Regardless, let it fly. It gets caught or it doesn’t. And maybe, just maybe, there’s a pass interference call in the end zone. (Since it wasn’t a classic Hail Mary situation, the usual PI rules would have applied.)

Whatever the chances of scoring would have been, it seemingly would have made MUCH more sense to throw the ball toward the ultimate destination than to hope a short pass would be the first domino to fall in a convoluted pattern that had a minuscule chance to working out.

As Simms said on PFT Live, that’s the play you run from your own 30, not the opponent’s 30.

At the opponent’s 30, you throw it to the end zone.

Again, it wasn’t as egregious as other blunders the Commanders have made this season. And it basically got lost in an otherwise nutty day.

It shouldn’t be lost on Commanders fans. The teams had a chance to score a touchdown that would have set up a one-point try for overtime or an all-or-nothing two-point conversion. Instead, they opted to trade in six the hard way for six the impossible way.

We’ll never know what would have happened if they’d just fired the ball the end zone. We know what happened when they didn’t. And it didn’t look like it ever had a real chance to deliver the touchdown the Commanders needed.

#2761. The Solar Report, Week 3: The Suns’ roller coaster is operating right on schedule

As I sit back and reflect on the third week of the NBA season, I find myself pondering the same question I ask every week: What did we learn?

And what does a team hovering around .500 look like? Inconsistent. There are going to be lapses in execution, questions about schematic philosophies, frustrating rotations, and stretches where the team struggles to establish any semblance of consistency. There will be games you believe Phoenix should win, only for one of those deficiencies to rear its ugly head and derail the evening. Conversely, there will be nights that appear to be scheduled losses, only for the Suns to exceed expectations and deliver a performance that reminds you why you were optimistic about them in the first place. That's the nature of a team living somewhere in the middle.

Yet because we experience the season one game at a time, dissecting every possession, rotation, adjustment, and coaching decision, our reactions tend to swing wildly from one extreme to the other. One night we're questioning the direction of the franchise, and the next we're convincing ourselves that perhaps this team has figured something out. It's an emotional roller coaster, and when you're invested in every outcome, it's difficult to avoid getting caught up in the moment. But when you pull back and examine the bigger picture, the trajectory of this team remains relatively aligned with what we believed it would be before the season began.

Granted, I don't think many of us anticipated this particular path. We might have expected different strengths, different weaknesses, or a more predictable formula for success. That's the beauty of an NBA season. There is no predetermined route to reaching your expectations. The journey reveals itself through the games, the adjustments, the unexpected contributions, and the opportunities that emerge along the way. And that's what makes watching it worthwhile.

The frustrations of one night and the elation of the next are all part of the experience. We can scrutinize the minutiae, debate what needs to change, and celebrate the moments when things finally click, but ultimately, the Suns are navigating a season that, so far, looks an awful lot like the one we anticipated.

It's also worth remembering that Phoenix hasn't exactly been handed an easy opening stretch. According to ESPN, the Suns have faced the toughest schedule in the NBA to begin the season. That context matters, particularly for a roster still developing chemistry, establishing rotations, and learning how to execute consistently within its systems.

Perhaps as that continuity develops, players accumulate more minutes together, and the schedule begins to soften, the Suns will find themselves moving closer to the winning percentage we expected when the season began.

Because while a 3-5 record might feel disappointing in the moment, it doesn't necessarily indicate that this team is falling short of its projected destiny. It might simply be the early turbulence that comes with being exactly the kind of team we thought it was. And that is what I learned this week.

We're beginning to see some progress from Khaman Maluach as the season continues. Much like our overall expectations for the Suns, inconsistency is going to be part of the equation, and that's perfectly understandable for a young player still learning how to navigate the NBA. His hands aren't always reliable, his positioning can be questionable, and there are moments when his inexperience is painfully evident. But his effectiveness, combined with his desire to compete, is creating opportunities, and he's beginning to capitalize on them.

When we look at his restocks per 36, the combination of rebounds, steals, and blocks, Maluach posted a total of 16.6 this past week, his highest weekly mark of the season. Much of that production came against the Houston Rockets, when he delivered a stellar performance in 18 minutes off the bench, grabbing 10 rebounds, blocking two shots, and recording a steal. That performance translated to an impressive 25.5 restocks per 36 minutes.

Now, you can certainly point to the fact that Houston was without Steven Adams and Clint Capela, which created a favorable opportunity for Maluach to make an impact. And you'd be correct. Their absence opened a door that might otherwise have remained closed. But here's the important part. Maluach walked through that door.

His rebounding percentage is gradually improving as well. Among NBA players who averaged at least 15 minutes per game this past week, Maluach ranked 22nd with a 16.6% rebound percentage. That same 16.6% mark leads the Suns for the season, further illustrating how valuable his presence can be on the glass for a team that desperately needs help in that department.

I  like the adjustment Jordan Ott has made by bringing Maluach off the bench. Do we ultimately want to see him become the starting center? Absolutely. But there's value in allowing him to develop in a role that better suits where he is right now. Oso Ighodaro provides greater offensive stability with his ability to facilitate and operate within the flow of the system, while his defensive versatility gives Phoenix more flexibility when switching assignments.

After all, the Suns' starting lineup with Maluach has posted a troubling -21 net rating. That's a significant indicator that the original configuration wasn't producing the desired results, regardless of how much we want to prioritize the rookie's development.

Ott deserves credit for recognizing that and making the adjustment. Bringing Maluach off the bench allows him to continue gaining valuable experience, capitalize on favorable matchups, and build confidence without the immediate responsibility of anchoring a starting unit that's still trying to establish its identity.It's an adjustment that benefits both the team and the player, and as Maluach continues to develop, those opportunities should only become more meaningful.

I used up my Ryan Dunn stat yesterday, and that was a good one. So I'll have to dig and find a different one…

Let's do this one: Devin Booker is 5th in the NBA in high-leverage points per game.

We know clutch, right? 5 minutes, 5-point margin. "High leverage" goes a bit beyond that. Per HoopsJunkie, "high leverage possessions are the moments in a game where the outcome hangs in the balance. These are the plays that can meaningfully swing a game's win probability and they tend to occur in close games as time winds down."

I recommend delving into their metrics to how they determine it, but the fact that Booker is 5th in the NBA in the metric is of note.

Four more games are on the slate for the Phoenix Suns in Week 4, beginning tonight against the San Antonio Spurs. This is a team that has won seven consecutive games after dropping its first two contests of the season, with its most recent victory coming against the Portland Trail Blazers. San Antonio is beginning to look like a machine, particularly with its three-guard combination of De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle, and Dylan Harper. That trio, alongside Devin Vassell and Victor Wembanyama, has produced a staggering +30.3 net rating in 100 minutes together. It's a lineup that presents problems on both ends of the floor, and Phoenix will have its hands full trying to slow it down.

After that, the schedule begins to lighten up a bit as the Suns host the Los Angeles Clippers on Tuesday night. The Clippers appear to be heading in the opposite direction of San Antonio, struggling to establish any meaningful momentum early in the season. And while Phoenix will be playing on the second night of a back-to-back, this is hopefully one of those opportunities where the Suns can take care of business without making things unnecessarily complicated.

Thursday brings a matchup against the Charlotte Hornets, along with an opportunity to welcome Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen back to the friendly confines of Phoenix. Despite the impressive individual performances we've seen from Allen, Charlotte has lost six consecutive games and currently sits at 3-7. A team that reached the Play-In Tournament last season appears to be heading in the wrong direction, making this another matchup where Phoenix should have an opportunity to capitalize.

The week concludes next Sunday when the Suns face the Los Angeles Lakers for the first time this season, closing out their current seven-game homestand. And the Lakers, led by Luka Doncic, have been absolutely eviscerating opponents offensively. Los Angeles leads the NBA in scoring at 122.0 points per game, while also ranking third in steals at 10.7 and third in blocks at 6.5.

So while much of the attention surrounding the Lakers understandably centers on Luka and their offensive firepower, their defensive production deserves recognition as well. They possess the ability to overwhelm opponents with their scoring while generating enough defensive disruption to create additional opportunities on the other end.

It's an interesting week ahead for Phoenix. The Spurs and Lakers present significant challenges, while the Clippers and Hornets offer opportunities to build momentum. If the Suns can continue developing the defensive identity we've witnessed over their past two victories, there's a chance to turn a difficult opening stretch into something that begins to resemble the team we expected entering the season.

Last week, the majority of the community voted that the Suns would finish 2-2. Where do they finish this week?

That's it for this week, Bright Siders. Stay frosty.

From there, the 49ers manhandled the Raiders. Yes, the Raiders scored another touchdown, but the 49ers were not blowing this lead. The win puts the 49ers at the No. 1 seed in the NFC, a half-game ahead of the Minnesota Vikings (6-1). They also lead the Seattle Seahawks and Los Angeles Rams by 2.5 games in the NFC West. Since both of those teams won, the lead stayed put, but the 49ers took care of business.

It came at a cost. Defensive tackle Gracen Halton broke his ankle and is out for the season. Cornerback Renardo Green also left with a back injury. Just when the pieces start coming back…

So that Minshew Magic we talked about last week? Well, it turns out that only lasts a single game.

Last Sunday, quarterback Gardner Minshew II came off the bench in Dallas with 1:35 left in the third quarter and the Cardinals down 17-3. He threw three fourth-quarter touchdown passes, won in overtime, and took the starting job. Like the Dallas game, Minshew found himself down 17-3, and unlike the Dallas game, we didn't get any fourth-quarter theatrics. We didn't even get a single touchdown. Instead, the Cardinals sat at three points.

That might be it for Minshew Mania, Magic, whatever we want to call it when he actually scores at least one touchdown.

Seattle had their own offensive issues. Drew Lock, or no Drew Lock, that seems a bit small, but the Seahawks found a way to win.

Minshew went 21-of-30 for 166 yards passing with no touchdowns and was sacked three times. Running back Tyler Allgeier ran for 147 yards in Dallas and managed 46 on 17 carries here. Meanwhile, Lock didn't turn the ball over and finished 19-of-28 for 175 yards and a touchdown.

The NFC West. Those games are slugfests. This one was a slugfest with 180 yards of penalties between the two teams. I guess it was entertaining?

#2759. Broncos and Bo Nix have won 16 straight one-score games

The Broncos keep finding ways to win games — especially close games.

Denver has won 16 straight games decided by one score or less. Quarterback Bo Nix has been the starter in each of the games.

Via NBC Sports research, the streak ties the 2023-24 Chiefs (with starting quarterback Patrick Mahomes) for the longest streak since 1950.

The Broncos last lost a one-score game in Week 3 of the 2025 season, 23-20 at the Chargers. Since then, the Broncos have won every one-score game in which they have played.

This year, they’re doing it despite being routinely outgained. For the season, they have a yardage differential of minus-658 — third worst in the NFL. And the Broncos have won three games in 2026 despite being outgained by 100 or more yards.

The record for any season is four wins, accomplished by eight different teams. With two more this year, the Broncos will have the record to themselves.

The next opportunity to win a one-score game comes on Sunday, at the Panthers in a rematch of Super Bowl 50.

#2758. Mushfiqur Rahim makes Bangladesh cricket history, becomes first to score 7,000 Test runs

Bangladesh veteran Mushfiqur Rahim added another landmark to his illustrious career, becoming the first batter from the country to score 7,000 runs in Test cricket. The 39-year-old achieved the milestone in the ongoing second Test against West Indies in Sylhet, further cementing his place among Bangladesh's greatest players in the longest format.Mushfiqur reached the landmark when he took a single off West Indies spinner Roston Chase to move to nine runs in his innings. The veteran initially appeared unaware of the achievement, but acknowledged the moment after his teammates rose from their seats in the dressing room to applaud him.The milestone was another reward for Mushfiqur's remarkable longevity and consistency in Test cricket. He had missed the opening Test of the series because of a finger injury but returned for the second match to add another chapter to his career.

Mushfiqur had already established himself as Bangladesh's leading Test run-scorer when he became the country's first batter to reach 5,000 runs in 2022 and 6,000 in 2024. He has now taken that record to another level, becoming the first Bangladesh player to breach the 7,000-run mark.He has accumulated 7,000 runs in his 107th Test, having needed only 25 innings to progress from 6,000 to 7,000. His tally includes 14 centuries, with his highest score being an unbeaten 219.Mominul Haque is second on Bangladesh's all-time Test run-scoring list with 5,293 runs, while former opener Tamim Iqbal is third. Mominul has scored 13 Test centuries, while Tamim has registered 10.Mushfiqur's latest achievement comes in a match in which his record for the highest individual score by a Bangladesh batter in Tests was surpassed. Towhid Hridoy struck an unbeaten 242 earlier in the ongoing Sylhet Test, going past Mushfiqur's previous best of 219 not out.

Having made his international debut in 2005, Mushfiqur is Bangladesh's most experienced Test cricketer. He became the first player from the country to feature in 100 Tests in November 2025 and is now appearing in his 107th match.His journey in the format has been one of steady evolution. Initially a lower-middle-order batter and wicketkeeper, Mushfiqur took 20 Tests to reach his first 1,000 runs. His batting responsibilities grew as he became a more established member of the side, particularly after taking over as Bangladesh captain in 2011.Over the years, he developed into one of the team's most dependable batters, producing crucial runs across conditions and against different opponents. His ability to maintain consistency over such a long career has been reflected in the latest milestone.

Mushfiqur has also made significant contributions in limited-overs cricket, scoring 6,697 runs in ODIs and 1,495 in T20 Internationals. He has since retired from both formats, with Test cricket remaining the stage on which he continues to extend his legacy.

#2757. Report: MRI shows Patrick Mahomes avoided serious injury

Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes underwent an MRI on his right elbow following Sunday’s 35-12 win over the Jets. The test did not reveal a major injury, Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports.

The team will monitor Mahomes’ strained elbow over the next few days for pain and swelling.

“If I’m able to play, I’m going to play,” Mahomes said, via Nate Taylor of ESPN. “That’s part of the game. It scares you in moments, when you get some pains in certain areas of your body. Obviously, it didn’t feel great, but I was able to kind of get it worked on a little bit, especially at halftime.”

With 1:33 left in the second quarter, Jets edge rusher David Bailey hit Mahomes’ right arm on a strip-sack. Will McDonald IV and Darrell Jackson Jr. also hit Mahomes on the play.

Mahomes did not miss any snaps despite the injury.

Julie Frymyer, an assistant athletic trainer for the team, spent halftime helping Mahomes get his right arm loose. Frymyer was also instrumental in Mahomes’ rehab of his left knee after the quarterback underwent major surgery on Dec. 15.

“Any time it’s elbows and knees, it’s always scary, just because you just don’t know,” Mahomes said. “Even my knee last year, after we were doing the initial test, I thought, because I could walk off the field, I was going to be good. Then, all of a sudden, you do one test, and you’re just out [for the rest of the season]. That stuff scares you. Once I could throw the ball, I knew it wasn’t a ligament, and it was more muscles.”

#2756. 10-game checkup: Wizards are better but the numbers contain some warnings

This season's Washington Wizards are better than the previous editions. They're 4-6, the vets have been good, a couple young guys look close to being good-to-really-good, and with the exception of the absolute dud against Oklahoma City, they've been fun to watch this season.

"The vets" in this case refers to Anthony Davis and Trae Young. While I have quibbles with how each of them are playing, it's more in the realm of nitpicking than major critiques. They've both been about as good as the Wizards could have reasonably expected.

Anthony Davis has anchored the Wizards' improved defense this season. | NBAE via Getty Images

Davis has anchored an improved defense — upgraded as much by his stellar communication as his rim protection capabilities. When he's on the floor, the team seems well organized and solid on the defensive end. In the two games he's missed, the Wizards defense essentially collapsed. That could partly be due to a step up in opponent quality, but I suspect not having Davis on the back line calling out actions is a big reason why.

Note: this is not a criticism directed at Alex Sarr, who has at times reminded me of Davis — in terms of positioning and movement — or even of Deandre Ayton. To say they're not as good as Davis at communicating on defense feels the stuff of Captain Obvious. Davis is an all-time defender, who has excelled at that aspect of a big man's defensive chores. In the case of Sarr, he's getting a crash course in being great on defense, and he has appeared more vocal than he was in previous seasons when Davis has been off the floor.

With Davis, my chief concern (aside from health) is on the offensive end, and it's really more about how they're using him than it is about Davis himself. Specifically, Davis leads the NBA in post-ups, and a hot game on the block got him all the way to 47th percentile in efficiency. The last time Davis was above average in post-up efficiency was 2023-24.

While I think it's possible to have a high-efficiency offense that leans heavily on a big man posting up — yes, even in this economy — I think that big man needs to be both efficient at scoring the ball and an effective passer. I don't think that description fits Davis.

As for Young, he's been a little above average in offensive efficiency despite shooting just 28.6% on threes so far this season. He's been a stellar set up man, and the combination of Young and Davis has helped make Washington a league leader in free throw attempts. Trips to the free throw line are second only to rim attempts in overall efficiency.

One of the good things about Young has been his defensive effort, which is dramatically improved from his days with the Atlanta Hawks. He still has lapses, and he'll always be a target because of his lack of size and strength, but he's competing on that end, and he's contributing with a handful of steals, deflections or well-timed traps per game.

Had I been writing an article like this after six games, I'd have been fretting about how none of the young guys looked like they were making The Leap. A couple terrific games from Kyshawn George gives Washington a candidate. He's still undermining his own value with rampant turnovers and excessive fouling, but he's big, physical, tough, competitive, and skilled. And he plays crazy hard, which is at once a strength and a potential weakness (to the extent that it leads to turnovers and fouls).

While I've had a vaguely disappointed feeling about Sarr's performance this season, the reality is he's been fine — about the same overall level of production as last season. That's not bad considering he missed most of the offseason with a broken foot and feels like he still needs some conditioning work.

Justin Champagnie was off to a terrific start before his foot injury. The Wizards definitely should want him to come back and stabilize their forward rotation before the postseason.

After missing the first four games with an ankle injury sustained in the preseason finale, AJ Dybantsa has been everything the Wizards could have hoped for. He's defended with intensity, and played with aggression on offense. One of my favorite plays from him so far this season was when he waved Davis out of the post so he could attack a mismatch.

Putting on my Shot Doctor coat, I think there's something off with Dybantsa's three-point shooting stroke, though I could be reaching. He hasn't hit threes yet, and his two-point percentage has been subpar, but both of those things are normal for rookies — even when they're going to be great in the future. He's shooting 79.3% from the free throw line, which suggests his shot isn't exactly broken.

The rest of the Wizards have varied between fine (Ayton) and not-so-good (Bub Carrington, Bilal Coulibaly, Tre Johnson, Will Riley, Khris Middleton). Brian Keefe and the coaching staff wisely dropped Middleton from the rotation.

Carrington has hit half his threes so far, and his defense is a lot better. He's also shot 2-12 on twos, and his non-three-point shooting contributions have been pretty minimal.

Coulibaly is a stellar defender who has utterly disappeared on offense. Teams are happy to let him shoot threes — they routinely leave him alone. So far this season, he's rewarded them with bricks. Last season, it seemed like he had an emergent driving game. Opposing defenders were having a tough time staying in front of him, even when they gave him a cushion. This season, he doesn't attack, even when he has a matchup advantage.

The most worrisome Coulibaly-related play of the year t0 my eye was when he got the ball in the dunker spot with Atlanta's CJ McCollum guarding him. Coulibaly was in great position, and he had a height and athleticism advantage on McCollum. He never looked to attack — just passed it back to Young on the perimeter. The possession cratered and the Wizards ended up with a turnover instead of a close-in shot in a mismatch.

My biggest concern is that the early returns suggest that the Wizards are weaker than their record indicates. The best indicator of relative team strength is strength of schedule adjusted scoring margin. The Wizards currently rank 27th in this metric. They ranked 24th before they got blown out by Oklahoma City.

So far this season, Wizards opponents have been outscored by 6.7 points per game. That group of opponents has outscored Washington by 4.7 points per game. That's not good.

For benchmarking purposes, here's where Washington ranks through 10 games in key statistical measures:

Offensive rating (points scored per 100 possessions): 22

Defensive rating (points allowed per 100 possessions): 18

Free throws made / field goal attempts: 11

On the offensive end, Washington is not shooting or rebounding well, but they're doing a good job avoiding turnovers and getting to the free throw line.

On defense, opponents are missing shots, which is the foundation of a good defensive team in the NBA. The Wizards are also doing a good job overall of not fouling. They're also not forcing turnovers, and they're getting beat on the boards.

One other key stat: 24.6. That's the Wizards' minutes-weighted average age so far this season — second lowest in the NBA this season.

Below is a first look at season-to-date scores in my Player Production Average metric. PPA accounts for each player's statistical contributions — each category weighted by how much it contributes to winning and losing. PPA is a per possession metric, which includes accounting for position, quality of competition while on the floor, and defensive impact. In PPA, 100 is average, higher is better, and replacement level is 45.

In most seasons, a PPA of 150 would put a player at least in the All-Star conversation. All-NBA level performances are typically 170 and above. It typically takes a score of 200 or better to merit MVP consideration.

ORTG is offensive rating — individual points produced per possession x 100. League average so far this season is 113.1.

#2755. Broncos Stock Up, Stock Down: Week 10 vs. Panthers

The Broncos did it again! After yet another 4th-quarter comeback, the Broncos won their 5th straight game with their victory over the Carolina Panthers and improved to 7-2 on the season. Like every Broncos game, this game was a rollercoaster from the start. They took an early 10-0 lead, but the Panthers came charging back and were on the verge of going up 21-13.

Devon Key's incredible interception flipped this game upside down and gave the momentum back to the Broncos, and they never looked back. Things did get tight there at the end, but Nik Bonitto called game with a clutch strip-sack, and the Broncos went on to celebrate another remarkable win.

Stock up and stock down is a weekly series where I go through the Denver Broncos' 53-man roster and tell you which Broncos players' stock is going up, down, or remains unchanged. After yet another 4th-quarter comeback and one-score victory, we have plenty of stocks trending in the right direction, with a few notable stocks going in the wrong direction.

Bo Nix – Stock up slightly: I thought Bo Nix played well overall on Sunday. He made some good throws and was leading the Broncos up and down the field against this Panthers secondary full of backups. However, he did have the interception and the off-target pitch late in the game. This was Nix's first interception since the one he threw vs. the Rams, where his arm was hit mid-throw, so I am not going to knock him too much for it.

I am going with stock slightly up. He threw for 237 yards and 2 touchdowns, which is a stat line I will take each and every week from Nix. He is beginning to look more and more like the quarterback we saw last season and I believe that will continue as the team emerges from their bye week.

Jarrett Stidham – Unchanged: Remains the Broncos veteran backup.

Sam Ehlinger – Unchanged: Remains the Broncos' third-string emergency quarterback.

Jonah Coleman – Stock up: The takeover has happened. Jonah Coleman played 58 of the 75 snaps on Sunday (77%) and was the unquestioned starter of the Broncos' backfield. He did not disappoint either. He had 17 carries for 57 yards, which is more of an offensive line problem than a running back problem (more on that later), but did score another touchdown and had an additional 4 receptions for 31 yards.

Altogether, he had 21 touches for 88 yards and a touchdown. A pretty solid showing for the Broncos rookie running back, but we'll have to see if they add to this running back room prior to the trade deadline this week.

JK Dobbins – Stock down: 4 carries for 18 yards and a 15% snap share.

That right there says it all. Dobbins has clearly fallen out of favor in the Broncos' backfield, and his time with the team could be coming to an end if they add another back at the deadline. We'll see what happens, but his role has significantly decreased since Jonah Coleman returned from injury.

Cody Schrader – Unchanged: Schrader was elevated from the practice squad but did not have a major role in Sunday's game.

Adam Prentice – Unchanged: Played 15 snaps on offense while also being a main contributor on special teams. He has his role on this team and he does it well.

Jaylen Waddle – Unchanged: This was going to be a big Jaylen Waddle game, but unfortunately, the Broncos' explosive wide receiver was knocked out of the game early after he suffered a concussion from a dirty hit by a Panthers defender.

Before he left the game, he had 1 catch for 22 yards and was destined for more.

Courtland Sutton – Stock up: I thought Sutton played solid on Sunday. It wasn't a huge game for the Broncos veteran wide receiver, but he led the wide receivers with 85% of the snaps and had 5 catches for 45 yards and a touchdown.

He caught everything thrown his way and made multiple big catches on third down for the Broncos. A solid overall showing.

Pat Bryant – Stock up: Welcome back, Pat Bryant! The Broncos' second-year wide receiver returned from IR before the game and made an immediate impact on the offense. He led the Broncos in receiving yards with 56 and had what ended up being the game-winning 26-yard touchdown late in the 4th quarter.

I think we will continue seeing Bryant make more and more impact plays as the season progresses.

Troy Franklin – Stock up: Like Sutton, I thought Troy played a solid overall game that nearly ended up being a big game. He finished with 3 catches for 31 yards, but had multiple clutch catches on third down late in the game. However, he nearly had a touchdown right before halftime, but a Panthers defender was able to knock the ball away. It was an incredible pass by Nix to Franklin who was open down the seam.

Marvin Mims – Unchanged: Mims did not do a whole lot on Sunday, but played his role. He saw limited snaps on offense but wasn't able to do much with them and continued being a kick return specialist for them.

Lil'Jordan Humphrey – Unchanged: He was inactive.

Adam Trautman – Stock up: He continues to lead the Broncos tight ends in snaps and has seen his role in the passing game increase a little bit in back-to-back games. He had a 20+ yard reception vs. the Chiefs and vs. the Panthers, he had 2 receptions for 15 yards.

Nothing to write home about, but the bar is low.

Evan Engram – Stock down: The stock down has little to do with his performance on Sunday, but more to do with the reports that the Broncos are looking to trade for a tight end. If they acquire a tight end, it will be a pass-catcher in all likelihood, which would negatively impact Engram's role and potentially even his roster spot. Now, nothing has happened, but the fact that they are looking isn't great for Engram.

On Sunday, Engram did have 4 catches for 33 yards, which is one of his better performances this season, so we'll see if anything changes here in the coming days.

Nate Adkins – Unchanged: Played 24% of the snaps on offense, but primarily played special teams and made a nice tackle on a return late in the game. He has his role, and he fills it well.

Dallen Bentley – Unchanged: Remained inactive.

Garett Bolles – Unchanged: Continues to be one of the better blindside protectors in the NFL.

Ben Powers – Stock down: The middle of the Broncos' line struggled on Sunday, and Powers was 50% of the problem. It's hard to get a run game going when you're allowing immediate pressure.

Luke Wattenberg – Stock down: Here is the other 50% of the problem. Wattenberg is praised for his intelligence, but he was knocked back a bit on Sunday and allowed immediate interior pressure. Both need to play better or it doesn't matter who our running back is.

Mike McGlinchey – Unchanged: Can't say I really noticed him positively or negatively on Sunday, which usually is a good thing.

Alex Palczewski – Unchanged: Played 5% of the snaps on Sunday, but maybe should see some time at left guard moving forward.

Matt Peart – Unchanged: Played on special teams.

Alex Forsyth – Unchanged: Played on special teams.

Kage Casey – Unchanged: The rookie remained inactive, but maybe should see time at left guard?

Zach Allen – Unchanged: I expected the defensive line to dominate a struggling Panthers offensive line, and that did not happen.

DJ Jones – Unchanged: Has been solid for the Broncos this season, but the Panthers had success on the ground vs. them.

Malcolm Roach – Unchanged: Has been a very underrated part of the Broncos' defensive line this season, but the unit struggled throughout most of the game.

Sai'vion Jones – Unchanged: Played 35% of the snaps and saw a minor boost in snaps with Uwazurike now on the IR.

Jordan Jackson – Unchanged: Was active and played 20% of the snaps.

Tyler Onyedim – Stock up: The Broncos' first selection of the 2026 NFL Draft was active for the first time this season and played 15% of the snaps.

Nik Bonitto – Stock up: The pass rush was frustratingly non-existent vs. the Panthers for most of the game, but Bonitto had a clutch strip-sack very reminiscent of Von Miller to end the game. A clutch game-winning and game-ending play.

Jonathon Cooper – Stock up: Cooper had a sack on Sunday and made life miserable for the Panthers rookie right tackle at times on Sunday. Still, the pass rush wasn't effective for most of the game, but his late-game play was nice to see.

Que Robinson – Stock up: He continues to make plays and flash his potential each and every week.

Dondrea Tillman – Unchanged: Plays his role and helps set the edge in the run game.

Alex Singleton – Stock down: After winning AFC Defensive Player of the Month this week, Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton had a tough showing vs. the Panthers. The missed tackles returned; he had issues in coverage and did not play as well as he did in the previous weeks.

Justin Strnad – Unchanged: I didn't notice Strnad much on Sunday, but the entire defense struggled at times vs. the Panthers, which was frustrating.

Jordan Turner – Unchanged: Played on special teams.

Karene Reid – Unchanged: Played on special teams.

Pat Surtain II – Unchanged: He did not let McMillian take over the game, but did give up a few plays throughout. Overall, the entire defense had issues on Sunday, but I am not concerned about PS2.

Riley Moss – Stock down: Moss suffered a scary concussion vs. the Panthers. It looked like he was knocked out after being kneed in the head, but thankfully he was able to get up and walk slowly to the locker room. Moss has dealt with multiple injuries this season and will have time to rest due to the much-needed bye week.

Ja'Quan McMillian – Unchanged: He had some issues in coverage too, but did have yet another clutch sack in the 4th quarter. Vance Joseph loves to blitz J-Mac in big moments, and he continues to come up big for them (PAY THAT MAN).

Jahdae Barron – Stock down: I have been a Barron supporter and thought he played well at times while Surtain was sidelined, but he had a bad showing vs. the Panthers. They targeted him in the passing game and continued to do so. The former first-round pick did not escape the whispers that he is a bust on Sunday after that showing.

Kris Abrams-Draine – Unchanged: Is dealing with an injury and was inactive.

Sean Fresch Jr. – Unchanged: Fresch was added to the 53-man roster and provided depth at corner and at returner. He had a nice return to open the game but, outside of that, did not play much.

Talanoa Hufanga – Unchanged: Was inactive but should be good to go after the bye week.

Brandon Jones – Unchanged: Was inactive, and we'll have to see how he's doing after the bye week.

Devon Key – Stock up: Key played just 36% of the defensive snaps on Sunday, but he had one of the biggest plays of the season thus far for the Broncos. He caught a deflected pass that was inches from touching the ground in the end zone in what ended up being a game-changing, momentum-swinging INT that helped the Broncos win that game. It'll be a play that will make the end-of-year highlights.

JL Skinner – Stock way up: After his big play vs. the Chiefs, I wondered if he would see more playing time, and boy, did he. Skinner got the start and played 91% of the defensive snaps. With Hufanga and Jones sidelined, this may have been an audition for Skinner.

Taylor Rapp – Unchanged: Rapp was released by the Broncos late in the week, but was signed back to the practice squad a day later. He has been elevated a max of three times now, so if the Broncos want to use him again this season, he will need to be re-added to the 53-man roster.

Tycen Anderson – Unchanged: Played on special teams.

Wil Lutz – Stock up: Went 2 for 2 on his field goal attempts and continued to be consistent for the Broncos.

Jeremy Crawshaw – Stock up: He booms them punts. Averaged 53.7 yards per punt and pinned the Panthers inside the 20 once.

Mitchell Fraboni – Unchanged: Good snaps.

#2754. Lawsuit is filed over shirtless Bill Belichick video

On Saturday, former Patriots coach Bill Belichick returned to New England, for a game between North Carolina and Connecticut. One day earlier, a lawsuit over a leaked video of a shirtless Belichick was filed in Massachusetts.

Via Edward Lewis of the California Post, Jordon Hudson (who either is dating or was dating Belichick) sued the owners of an Airbnb rental for disclosing the Ring camera video generated three years ago, when Hudson and Belichick were using the property.

The legal argument seems to be that the owners, by disclosing the video of Belichick sans shirt, triggered a storm of unflattering scrutiny of Hudson.

From the lawsuit: “As a result of this leak, numerous false tabloid-like and click-bait stories have, and continue to, be published about her, which have held her up to intense ridicule and derision and caused immense damage.”

The entire premise of the lawsuit seems to be that the leak “outed [Hudson’s] romantic relationship with Belichick, something she had worked hard to keep private.” One of the basic factual questions will be whether she behaved in a manner consistent with keeping her identity as Belichick’s secret girlfriend private.

At some point, she wasn’t keeping it private. She was flaunting it.

By filing the lawsuit, Hudson has pulled the pin on a grenade that may eventually throw shrapnel at Belichick. If, as it appears, she believes that she never would have gotten her 15 minutes (and then some) of infamy without the video of shirtless Bill being leaked, it will be fair for the defendants’ lawyers to aggressively explore all of the ways in which she seemingly sought out attention and/or notoriety.

The lawsuit ultimately sets the stage for a potentially aggressive discovery process that will most likely include lengthy depositions of Hudson and Belichick.

And, during the lawyer-controlled question-and-answer sessions, Hudson will not be able to blurt out, “We’re not answering that.”

As it relates to Belichick, the lawsuit creates potential hassle, headache, and distraction. He should have tried to talk her out of doing it.

Maybe he did. If he did, he failed miserably.

#2751. Bucks vs. Celtics Player Grades: Centre rotation goes from bad to worse in rout

After a blinding start in which they led by 14 early, the Milwaukee Bucks ultimately succumbed to the Boston Celtics, losing 117-97. Put simply, the Celtics were the more physical team, and they dictated the game for most of it. A key reason for this was that Milwaukee's primary big men were both horrendous, so much so that Jenkins turned to Jericho Sims in the second half over Kel'el Ware. I will say that the C's made a bunch of tough shots—Paul George in particular—and you can't really do much about that. Read our full summary of the game here and catch a six-minute audio recap on the Bucks+ podcast, Bucks In Six Minutes, below.

20 minutes, 7 points, 5 rebounds, 6 assists, 1 steal, 3 turnovers, 2/4 FG, 2/3 3P, -7

Rollins wasn't horrible, but like Jakucionis, he just couldn't find any separation to attack. And when he did try to attack, he was swallowed up and turned the ball over, or he threw a grenade to someone else. I also didn't feel like Rollins' point-of-attack defence was any great shakes.

26 minutes, 13 points, 2 assists, 1 turnover, 5/12 FG, 1/5 3P, -3

The Celtics seemed much more prepared for Herro than they were for the last matchup, picking him up higher on the floor and waiting more intently in the gaps. They wanted to squeeze the floor on Herro, make him a passer, and bet they could recover to shooters, which they did for the most part. Again, Herro is not a real number one option, and when he comes up against teams who can send guys in waves at him, this can be the result. Not sure how much the knee injury—which he did come back and play with—impacted his performance.

22 minutes, 4 points, 2 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 1/3 FG, 0/2 3P , 4/4 FT, -6

Jaquez just made no impact whatsoever. Had no ability even to generate shots, let alone make them. At least he wasn't just chucking for the hell of it, though. Jaquez was tasked with guarding Paul George and got lit up, but honestly, I thought a lot of PG's shots were well contested.

31 minutes, 27 points, 4 rebounds, 0 assists, 1 steal, 2 blocks, 1 turnover, 10/17 FG, 6/13 3P, -4

Kuzma started like a house on fire with 16 points in the first quarter, then scored 11 for the rest of the game. I liked his shot selection to start the game, which helped him get hot and then make a few tough ones. However, once you miss your second heat check, it's time to put the cue in the rack and run real offence. Kuzma didn't do that; he took like three or four horrendous shots in the first quarter while the floor wasn't set, which is exactly what allowed the Celtics to get back into the game so quickly. To be clear, Kuzma was far from the biggest issue, but his recklessness late in the quarter sullied his terrific start. On the plus side, his defence on Tatum was excellent for majority of the game.

24 minutes, 3 points, 5 rebounds, 7 assists, 1 block, 2 turnovers, 1/8 FG, 0/3 3P, -3

I mean, while he contributed in other areas—including getting four of his seven assists in the first quarter—this was, by and large, another horrendous game from Turner, who once again looked like a boy among men. And it's not like he was matching up with Hakeem Olajuwon; this was Neemias Queta, who, with all due respect, is a low-end starter. Turner had some truly horrendous sequences where he looked a step late on every decision. I hate to get into these areas, but Turner doesn't look fit to me; he looks out of shape and is moving worse than he did even last year.

9 minutes, 0 points, 0 rebounds, 0/2 FG, -15

I've seen some online chatter about whether Ware should start over Turner, and honestly, I'm not on board because he's been even worse! Struggling to catch basic passes, poor drop defence in the pick-and-roll, and no rebounding presence. Didn't play in the second half, and rightfully so.

7 minutes, 1 point, 2 rebounds, 2 turnovers, 0/1 FG, 0/1 3P, -11

Jakucionis struggled to get anywhere; he looked outmatched by the Celtics' physical guards, which is exactly what happened when they last played Boston.

28 minutes, 13 points, 8 rebounds, 4 assists, 1 block, 1 turnover, 5/11 FG, 1/4 3P, -12

As usual, Burries made an impact as a rebounder, with four of his eight boards coming on the offensive glass. Also got to some great mid-range looks against a bevy of tough defenders. Remains a struggle from three, but that will come. Yet again, Burries was one of the biggest cheerleaders from the bench; doesn't go unnoticed.

18 minutes, 5 points, 2/6 FG, 1/5 3P, -21

Made a nice up-and-under move, but otherwise nothing all that noteworthy from Green in this one.

23 minutes, 12 points, 5 rebounds, 1 steal, 5/9 FG, 2/4 3P, -14

Another solid game for Ament, who punished the Celtics for helping off him. I said before the season that Ament had to find his niche as an NBA player, and the path of least resistance was to build from the outside in; well, he seems to be doing that. I've also noted that I wanted to see Ament make teams feel his presence more, and he's starting to do that. Showed some great stuff as a rebounder, grabbing two O-boards and putting shots back in around the rim, along with a nice finish in traffic and more great wing defence possessions guarding Tatum.

15 minutes, 10 points, 3/3 FG, 2/2 3P, -2

A nice get-right game for Dieng, who finally saw the ball go through the hoop in this one. He didn't show much of the enticing creation ability we saw toward the back end of last season—mainly because the ball wasn't really in his hands—but it was a nice starting point for Dieng to build confidence.

I thought Sims gave them a defensive boost; he also set solid screens to get guys open and moving downhill. Shot a three, which was interesting. Other than that, nothing much to report.

Let's move off the bigs and talk about the guard rotation. They've struggled to get multiple of the four guards—Herro, Burries, Rollins, and Jakucionis—working well together. I understand starting Herro and Burries for a range of reasons, but neither is a true point guard, and there seems to be a weird push-and-pull where neither feels like they can play their natural game. I don't love the fit, but I also don't know that I'd mess with it; after all, the team has started great in each of the last two games. That said, I do think that getting Rollins more minutes alongside one or both of these players would have a net positive effect on the team (even if their individual scoring numbers might go down). Of course, they're also trying to play Jakucionis, whose minutes are dwindling by the game. Honestly, I might sit KJ completely for a few games, give his minutes to Rollins, and see if that works. The other option would be sitting Green, but he's been largely quite good, so that feels undeserved (plus, I think they'd like to keep Green in the rotation for trade value purposes). In any event, Jenkins needs to find answers for the lack of overall guard production in recent games, even though, yes, there's no panacea staring him in the face. I would also look at incorporating more sets to get the guards going downhill more and playing one-on-one less; things have felt pretty stagnant at times over the last few games.

Inactive: Kam Jones, Cormac Ryan, Pete Nance, Bogoljub Markovic, Gary Trent Jr.

A key reason the Bucks can struggle to rebound—despite being a good rebounding team overall—is personnel. Turner seems to have lost much of his athleticism, Sims is undersized, and Ware's attitude can wax and wane. When they're not relying on their team-wide concepts (gang crashing, tagging up), they can get found out.

Jenkins said they will evaluate how Tyler Herro feels today after a Celtics player landed on his knee. They don't think it's anything serious, but it sounds like missing a game or two is possible.

Jenkins was much more subdued at last night's presser than at the last game's, highlighting the good things his team did to build the initial lead rather than the bad things they did to give it up.

Jenkins also backed Turner, pointing out his non-scoring contributions: "He's just going through a rough patch right now… Two games ago against Boston, he had a heck of a game. He's just got to stay the course."

Jakucionis' minutes over his last three games: 12, 10, and seven.

From the end of the first to the start of the second, Boston went on an 18-0 run.

Interior defence was an issue yet again; the Celtics destroyed the Bucks 44-28 in that area.

The Bucks travel to the Big Apple today to face the New York Knicks on Tuesday night. Watch at 6:30 p.m. CST on MY24.

#2749. Norwich form 'reminder of how good we can be'

Norwich City defender Harry Darling said the Canaries' fourth consecutive Championship win was a reminder "of how good we can be".

Philippe Clement's side's 5-0 win at Bristol City followed a 4-0 win at Derby County in midweek and has lifted the Norfolk side up to 12th in the table.

Their winning run, which has also seen them come from behind to beat Charlton Athletic and Watford, has seen Clement's team move from being one point outside the relegation zone to 11 points clear and only three short of the final play-off place.

Darling, who scored Norwich's second at Ashton Gate, said: "After the Derby game, we wanted to back it up again and it was a really good performance."

Since fighting back from 2-0 down to beat Watford on 31 October, Norwich have now scored 12 unanswered goals in three matches.

"To be honest I'm more buzzing about the clean sheets," Darling told BBC Radio Norfolk.

"We haven't been good enough, especially at the start of the season with goals, and to get back-to-back clean sheets was a really big goal for us.

"On the back of last year, we know how good we can be. Obviously we didn't show that at the start of the season and we weren't good enough. It's nice to get back to where we were a little bit - we just want to keep pushing on."

#2748. 2026-27 NBA Power Rankings Week 4: 76ers move into top spot, focus on unexpected standouts

This week's NBC Sports NBA Power Rankings see some teams we expected to be in the top 10 all season move back in: San Antonio, Oklahoma City. Philadelphia takes over the top spot as it keeps finding ways to win.

This week we will focus on an unexpected standout for each team, guys who might not always get the shine they deserve but contribute a lot to winning for their teams.

Record: 9-2Ranking last week: No. 3Games this week: Boston, Toronto, Indiana

Unexpected standout: VJ Edgecombe. Starting with four other future Hall of Famers (a bit of projection, but not crazy), Edgecombe has accepted being a role player, doing whatever needs to be done to win, and yet we still get chances to see him showcase his talent. "I think his role has shifted a little bit for us this year in that one of the things at the top of his priority list is to supply energy," 76ers head coach Nick Nurse told NBC Sports Philadelphia. "He's the youngest of the crew. He's got to have explosive energy at the start of most games. And it's a little shift for him because he was playing super huge minutes … last year. He doesn't have the ball in his hands as much, so he's got to go get it and find it... And he's probably going to be [defending] the best backcourt player. Him coming out with that kind of spark is what we need."

Record: 8-2Ranking last week: No. 7Games this week: at Phoenix, at Chicago, Golden State, at Utah

Unexpected standout: Julian Champagnie. He's not really an unexpected standout, but is there one on a high-profile team that was in the NBA Finals last June? When Mitch Johnson decided to start three guards — De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle, and Dylan Harper — Julian Champagnie was the odd man out and got pushed to the bench. He's handling it like a pro, and he's still producing, shooting 42% from 3, giving them almost 10 points a night, and defending well.

Record: 9-2Ranking last week: No. 6Games this week: at Atlanta, at Milwaukee, at Phoenix

Unexpected standout: Walker Kessler. I seriously considered one of or a combination of, the three wings who have played well for the Lakers this season — Ziaire Williams, Jake LaRavia and Matisse Thybulle — but the reality is their perimeter, turnover-forcing defense isn't possible without a high-level rim protector in the paint. So far this season, Kessler has proven to be the big man the Lakers need him to be (and paid him to be). He has thrived rolling to the rim and finishing passes from Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves. The Lakers are clicking, and none of it works on either end without Kessler. Also, this is why they paid Austin Reaves so much money this summer:

Record: 8-2Ranking last week: No. 4Games this week: at Philadelphia, at Toronto, Dallas

Unexpected Standout: Luka Garza. At some point, Joe Mazzulla just needs to give Garza a chance. Last season, Garza got bumped down the center pecking order when Boston traded for Nikola Vucevic, at least until deep in the playoffs when Mazzulla was forced to give Garza a chance. This offseason, Boston spent money on Mitchell Robinson, but in his limited minutes (13 a night so far), Garza is giving the Celtics 7.3 points, 3.7 rebounds and, unlike Mitchell, he can space the floor with his shooting (54.2% from 3 so far this season, which is inflated, but defenders have to respect the shot). Garza has developed his game and deserves more run.

Record: 8-2Ranking last week: No. 11Games this week: at Portland, at Portland, at LA Clippers, at Sacramento

Unexpected standout: Aday Mara. When I watched Aday Mara struggle at Summer League last July, I thought the Michigan center would need a season or two in the Thunder development program to be NBA-ready. Then there he was on opening night, blocking Victor Wembanyama at the rim and already in the rotation. Mara is playing nearly 20 minutes a night off the bench — taking on a larger role while Chet Holmgren is out — and averaging 8.1 points and 5.9 rebounds a game. Sam Presti nails another draft pick.

Record: 8-3Ranking last week: No. 13Games this week: Dallas, Chicago

Unexpected standout: Ayo Dosumnu. Since Anthony Edwards went out for knee surgery, Dosumnu has been the best and most consistent Timberwolves player, averaging 17.3 points, 5 rebounds, and 4.3 assists while shooting 42.5% from 3-point range. Dosumnu was my preseason Sixth Man of the Year pick, but with Anthony Edwards out he's going to get too many starts, still, he's the guy keeping the Timberwolves afloat.

Record: 6-3Ranking last week: No. 2Games this week: Washington, at Washington, at Miami

Unexpected standout: Paul Reed. With Jalen Duran out, Reed has stepped up on both ends of the floor and is currently the Pistons' third-leading scorer. He has so much craft to his game. He's finding a way to get to 12.8 points and 6.8 rebounds a game, and with him and the expected elite play from Cade Cunningham, the Pistons don't miss a beat. This team remains a regular-season juggernaut.

Record: 7-3Ranking last week: No. 1Games this week: Denver, Golden State, Utah, at Washington

Unexpected standout: Fred VanVleet. This wasn't unexpected to everyone, some of us have been saying since early in the summer that VanVleet's return and role as floor general was going to solve a lot of problems in Houston. It has. The Rockets are playing at a faster tempo while turnovers are down, spacing is far better in the half-court offense, and VanVleet understands how to manipulate a defense to get the ball to plays in spaces that play to their strengths. He's the reason the Rockets have the second best offense in the NBA early this season.

Record: 7-3Ranking last week: No. 12Games this week: New Orleans, at Houston, at San Antonio

Unexpected standout: Yaxel Lendeborg. Nobody saw a 24-year-old rookie stepping in and being the secondary scoring option the Warriors needed next to Stephen Curry, but here we are. Lendeborg is the two-timeline guy the Warriors needed. Here is Curry on Lendeborg: "He's just got composure, feel. His size on the court, he's a matchup problem. He's never really in a hurry, and he's starting to see the pictures really well. Distributing, being aggressive, getting to the free-throw line, offensive rebounding. Kind of the full package. So, we want him to continue to play aggressive."

Record: 5-4Ranking last week: No. 15Games this week: Milwaukee, Cleveland, at Indiana, at Toronto

Unexpected standout: Landry Shamet. I'm not sure there actually can be an unexpected standout on the defending NBA champions, a team in the nation's largest media market, where even casual fans know the role players, but if we have to go with one, we go with Shamet. Nobody is smarter off the ball at confusing defenders and finding space to get off his shot (or draw a foul). Check out Fred Katz's great breakdown of Shamet's game at The Athletic. Shamet rarely starts but he's fifth on the team in scoring and defenders are told not to lose him on the perimeter or he will make them pay.

Record: 6-3Ranking last week: No. 9Games this week: Oklahoma City, Oklahoma City, at Sacramento

Unexpected standout: Toumani Camara. He was already an All-Defensive player and one of the league's best on-ball defenders, able to lock guys down 1 through 5. However, this year Toumani Camara has put the "3" in 3&D and is hitting 45.2% of the more than seven 3-pointers he is taking a game. With that, he becomes a key part of what Portland is building around slashers like Ja Morant (once he gets healthy) and Deni Avdija.

Record: 5-5Ranking last week: No. 8Games this week: at Charlotte, at New York, at Miami, Dallas

Unexpected Standout: Mario Hezonja. Anyone who remembers Hezonja from his first five years in the league — drafted No. 5 by Orlando in 2015 and playing for the Magic, Knicks and Trail Blazers before washing out of the league — may not recognize him after six years in Europe. Most notably, the skinny 6'8" wing has filled out and is bigger, stronger and knows how to use that. Also, the kid who wanted to be the playmaker has accepted a 3&D role and is thriving off the bench for Cleveland this season. It's a great story, and he's been important to the Cavs this season.

Record: 5-4Ranking last week: No. 14Games this week: Memphis, Boston, at Philadelphia, New York

Unexpected standout: Immanuel Quickley. If you wanted to see how much Immanuel Quickley matters to this team, watch the fourth quarter of the Raptors' come-from-behind win against the Clippers from a week ago. Quickley had 14 points, attacking and getting to the line and also hitting a 3. Like all the Raptors, he's also a plus defender. In his seventh NBA season, the guard is giving Toronto 17.4 points and nearly six assists a game, and he's part of what makes this team dangerous (when Kawhi Leonard is healthy).

Record: 6-3Ranking last week: No. 5Games this week: at Toronto, Denver, at New Orleans, Brooklyn

Unexpected standout: Ty Jerome. The long-time darling of the analytics community, Jerome has shown this potential at times — he averaged 19.7 points a game last season, but he played only 15 games — but this season he is an offensive juggernaut, averaging 26.6 points per game and shooting 36.4% from 3-point range. There are so many Grizzlies who could be spotlighted here, and I seriously considered Zach Edey, who is quietly central to this team, as well as Cedric Coward. But Jerome is the definition of an unexpected standout.

Record: 5-4Ranking last week: No. 16Games this week: at Houston, at Memphis, at New Orleans

Unexpected Standout: Trevon Brazile. It's a little difficult to find a player in Denver playing well outside of Nikola Jokic and Jamal Murray, which is part of the problem. However, Brazile, the rookie out of Arkansas, has been that guy, averaging 8 points and 6.4 rebounds a night in 22 minutes and bringing a much-needed burst of athleticism to the team. He said it took a minute to get used to the spacing and style of the NBA game. "It's just learning where to go on the floor, it's different from college," Brazile said. "In college I was just trying to run in the rim. You know, I get a lob or something, but you know, it's different type of space in the NBA."

Record: 7-4 Ranking last week: No. 18 Games this week: Los Angeles Lakers, at Chicago, at Milwaukee

Unexpected Standout: Aaron Wiggins. It's too early to talk about end-of-season awards, but if we did, Wiggins might be the frontrunner for Six Man of the Year, averaging 14.9 points and 3.7 rebounds a game off the bench, and the team is outscoring opponents when he is on the floor (and they are slightly in the negative when he is not). Special shout-out to Nickeil Alexander-Walker, who could have qualified here and should be an All-Star this year but doesn't get thought of that way.
