#2679. NFL trade deadline 2026: Ranking 20 players who could have the biggest impact if dealt

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL trade deadline is on our doorstep. General managers and front-office personnel now need to take a hard look at their franchise and ask themselves what's best at this pivotal milestone. Do they hold firm, feeling like what they've put together is suitable for the rest of the stretch run? Do they sell after an uninspired start that has no reprieve in sight, shifting the focus beyond 2026? Do they buy, hoping that move could springboard them to glory? Those are the discussions happening right now.

Let's play in the buyer's sandbox for this discussion. No deal is equal. Some could simply be to add depth, while others are a swing-for-the-fences move, similar to what we've already seen from Chicago, when they shipped two first-rounders for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. Below are 20 players who've been spinning in the rumor mill, ranked by the impact they could make if dealt to a new team.

Potential landing spots: Packers, Patriots, Broncos

After Philadelphia dropped to 2-7 with a loss to the Giants, everything should be on the table. That includes moving on from Pro Bowl guard Landon Dickerson, who has been among the Eagles players reportedly mulled over in trade talks. Philadelphia's offensive line has already seen big shakeups with Lane Johnson retiring and Cam Jurgens traded. It's possible Howie Roseman continues to gain future draft capital amid a lost season. While a guard doesn't exactly move the needle in terms of making headlines, Dickerson could be a true game changer for a playoff hopeful that needs help on the interior. That said, the 28-year-old has struggled this season. On top of missing time due to injury, Dickerson has allowed a sack in each of his four games played this season, so there is some risk for any team acquiring him. Meanwhile, Philadelphia could look to move on from Dickerson, with his cap number rising to $13.7 million and $17.7 million over the final two years of his contract.

Potential landing spots: Chiefs, Commanders, Rams

Jeudy isn't as high-profile a name as some other wideouts on the trade block, but he's still a quality pass catcher that could help deepen a room. This season, Jeudy has been buried on the Browns depth chart behind rookie Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion, but flashed when his number is called. He's signed through 2027 with a base salary of just $1.5 million, so he'd be a cheap piece that could help a team for the stretch run of 2026 and beyond if they'd like.

Potential landing spots: Lions, Bills, Panthers

Woolen is playing on a one-year, $15 million contract. With free agency looming, he'd be a natural trade chip as Philadelphia sits at 2-7 as the deadline arrives. The 27-year-old corner is allowing a 51% completion rate when targeted this season, along with a career-high 99.9 passer rating. While the four touchdowns allowed isn't great, Woolen is a quality corner, which has plenty of value on the trade market. He also had a 73.6 passer rating allowed last season in Seattle, so there is the possibility that a change of scenery helps bring his production back to that level. Teams are always searching for help in the secondary, and if Woolen has the ceiling, to help be a steady piece for the stretch run.

Potential landing spots: Vikings, Giants, Broncos

Pollard isn't in the same tier as the likes of Jonathan Taylor or Derrick Henry. That said, the Titans back has been balling out in recent weeks leading up to Tennessee's Week 9 bye. Over his past two games alone, Pollard has rushed for 246 yards on a 5.3 yards-per-carry average to go along with five rushing touchdowns. The 29-year-old also caught six of his eight targets over that stretch for 46 yards. While he won't rush for over 100 yards in every game he plays down the stretch, he'd be an underrated addition for a team that is looking for a boost to its rushing attack. He's also set to be a free agent at the end of this season, so he may not cost as much as some other backs rumored to be available given his rental status.

Potential landing spots: Cowboys, Patriots, Packers

With the Chargers season already upside down, he'd be a fascinating addition for any team looking to bolster its pass rush. After all, the 2023 second-round pick recorded 13 sacks in 2025. He's only 24 years old, so he'd likely be hard to pry out of Los Angeles. However, Tuipulotu will be a free agent at the end of this season. If the Chargers don't have any plans to re-sign him, it'd be a logical move to see what they can get for him.

Potential landing spots: Broncos, Vikings, Seahawks

The veteran tight end is a solid pass catcher. Goedert signed a one-year, $7 million contract extension with the Eagles back in March and is set to be a free agent at the end of the season. If they can get more for him now than the compensatory selection they'll eventually receive if he signs elsewhere, it'd be a solid move for Howie Roseman. Goedert is also no stranger to playing on the big stage, suiting up in 13 playoff games over the course of his career and catching 56 balls for 595 yards and five touchdowns.

Potential landing spots: Bengals, Vikings, Giants

The Jets have been adamant that they won't move Hall before the deadline, but many will still inquire. That's especially true after the Week 9 loss to Kansas City that dropped them to 2-7 on the season. In that defeat, Hall led the team with 15 carries and rushed for 61 yards. That 4.1 yards-per-carry average was mirrored by fellow back Braelon Allen, who finished with 33 yards on eight carries. When Hall was sidelined the previous five games with an injury, Allen shined in the starting role, which should make Hall expendable at the right price. While Hall is more of a luxury piece on New York's roster, he'd be a bellcow back on most other rosters and could be the missing piece for contenders that are looking for some backfield help.

Potential landing spots: Bills, Commanders

Hooker has been putting together a career year with Tennessee so far. The veteran safety has five interceptions through seven games, which already ties his career high. He's also on pace to set career marks in total tackles and pass breakups. Before the bye week, Hooker showed his worth to a secondary with a three-interception performance against Joe Burrow and the Bengals in Week 8. Through seven games, he's allowed a 71.3 passer rating against. Hooker, a fourth-round pick in 2019, may be one of the more underrated pieces at the deadline, but his playmaking ability shouldn't be overlooked. His knack for creating turnovers could prove to be huge for a playoff contender. The only thing that may hamper his trade market is his contract, as he's under team control through 2028, but his cap hits are $13.1 million and $16.3 million over the next two seasons. Strictly looking at his play, however, he's a playmaker.

Potential landing spots: Chiefs, Patriots, 49ers

Downs has requested a trade out of Indianapolis, so he could be one of the names that actually gets moved before the deadline. The 2023 third-round pick out of UNC started to break out with an 803-yard sophomore season in 2024, but has quite made the leap most hoped he would to this point. Of course, part of that has been due to the Colts' continued issues at quarterback. He's shown the ability to create separation, and if he ends up on a team with better play under center, Downs could finally reach his ceiling. He's also set to be a free agent at the end of this season, so he may not cost much as a rental, making him attractive to a slew of receiver-needy teams.

Potential landing spots: Cowboys, Packers, Bills

Sweat logged 12 sacks for the Cardinals in 2025, so he's shown a strong ability to disrupt the quarterback. Pass rushers are always going to be a sought-after piece at the deadline, and with Arizona under .500, it'd made sense for them to deal away Sweat before Tuesday. That's especially true considering he has no guaranteed money remaining on his contract (that runs through 2028) beyond this season. That means Sweat will likely seek a revised contract. Inking a soon-to-be 30-year-old pass rusher doesn't seem like the most pressing need for a still-rebuilding Cardinals squad. Sweat is also no stranger to playing in big games, notably recording 2.5 sacks in Philadelphia's win over the Chiefs in Super Bowl LIX.

Baker is signed through 2027 and will turn 31 in January. With Arizona sitting in last place in their division, it makes sense that this would be a player they'd look to move for future draft capital at the deadline. Baker would be a fascinating addition to any defense as he's such a versatile weapon. The safety can play deep as well as near the line of scrimmage and is good against the run. He's a four-time All-Pro, but has only played in one playoff game in his career. Landing with a playoff contender and making a postseason run could spark the veteran.

Potential landing spots: Chiefs, 49ers, Raiders

Thomas looked like he was going to be the latest LSU receiver to take the league by storm with his 1,200-yard rookie season in 2024. Since then, however, the former first-round pick has fallen off dramatically and has been at the center of trade rumors this cycle. That's especially after he played just 19 snaps in Jacksonville's Week 9 win over the Ravens. While Thomas's production has fallen, he's still only 24 years old, and we've seen him dominate in the NFL before. It's possible he simply needs a change of scenery to tap back into that rookie version of himself. If he does and lands with a team like Kansas City or San Francisco, he could help shift the balance of power in the Super Bowl race.

Potential landing spots: Bears, Bills, Cowboys

Los Angeles is going nowhere fast in 2026 as they sit in last place in the AFC West, which makes any veteran -- especially someone like Mack -- subject to a slew of trade rumors. The Chargers have reportedly been unwilling to engage in trade talks despite their lackluster start to the season, but reality needs to set in at some point. Mack is much more valuable to them as a trade chip than an edge defender on the field, especially as he's on a one-year deal. A team acquiring Mack would get a future Hall of Fame talent that is still able to pressure the quarterback in what could be the final chapter of his career.

Potential landing spots: Vikings, Seahawks

Jones' name appearing in the rumor mill was a bit of a surprise, seeing as the Colts signed him to a two-year, $88 million extension. However, they should be exploring all of their options amid a 2-7 start and the recent firing of GM Chris Ballard. If they can get something for him and get out from under his contract, it could be a worthwhile endeavor. While Jones hasn't been able to recapture his magic from the first half of last season, he could be a solid option for a team like the Minnesota Vikings, who are dealing with an injury to Kyler Murray. Jones has familiarity with the organization as he spent time with them in 2024. If he ended up with Minnesota, he'd be one of the biggest wild cards of the second half of the season.

Potential landing spots: Patriots, Vikings, Giants

Baltimore is reportedly not expected to trade Henry before Tuesday's deadline, but his name has been in rumors. After all, the Ravens are last in the AFC North following their loss to the Jaguars, which dropped them to 4-5 on the season. The trade for Jacoby Brissett, alongside the hope that Lamar Jackson (fractured right thumb) could return late in the year, suggests they won't sell at the deadline, but it's not out of the realm of possibility they get a Godfather offer for Henry and have a serious conversation about moving him. Henry is set to turn 33 in January and is signed through 2027, but has no guaranteed money left on his deal beyond 2026. He could be more valuable to the franchise as a trade chip, and he'd be a remarkable addition to an RB-needy playoff contender for the stretch run.

Potential landing spots: Broncos, Vikings, Bengals

It does seem like the Eagles will listen to most players on the roster, but they're reportedly not looking to deal Barkley. Again, maybe that's simply because the right offer hasn't come across Howie Roseman's desk yet. Barkley is set to turn 30 years old this offseason, and injuries have started to pile up for the veteran back, so it'd make sense if they explored moving him, especially if they are on the verge of a reset following this 2026 season. Barkley would be one of the biggest midseason additions this cycle and, if he can stay healthy, completely changes the dynamic of how teams would defend whichever offense he'd end up on.

Potential landing spots: Chiefs, Raiders, 49ers

Wilson missed New York's Week 9 loss to the Chiefs due to a concussion, so teams looking to deal for him would have to be comfortable with his status going forward. That said, Wilson is one of the most underrated receivers in the NFL and would become a superstar if he fell in the right situation. Despite having lackluster QB play throughout his career, Wilson has three 1,000-yard seasons under his belt. He'd be a No. 1 option in most offenses and take any unit he'd land with to a new level. The question is whether or not the Jets would actually move Wilson. Despite plenty of speculation, they're reportedly not interested in dealing him. That said, if a team comes to them with a massive offer, at 2-7, they'd have to consider it.

Potential landing spots: Cowboys, Lions, Bills

The Raiders already traded Crosby once -- dealing him to the Ravens this offseason before the trade was nullified due to his physical -- so they could absolutely trade him again. Crosby is one of the league's top pass rushers and would be an all-in move for any team pulling off a blockbuster to trade for him. He won't come cheap, but Crosby is a disruptive force off the edge, which is immensely valuable come the postseason. The 29-year-old -- who is signed through 2028 -- dramatically improves any defense.

Potential landing spots: Vikings, Broncos, Bengals

Taylor didn't exactly make an exclamation point in Indy's Week 9 loss to the Cowboys to convince teams to go out and trade for him. He rushed for just 46 yards on 13 carries, while catching five of his six targets for 18 yards. That said, we all know that Taylor is one of the best backs in the NFL when he's firing on all cylinders. The Colts are about to hit the full reset button this offseason after falling flat with a 2-7 record so far in 2027. Taylor no longer fits their timeline and is better served as a trade chip to get assets rather than compete in the current moment. Taylor is a complete back who could have a Christian McCaffrey-like impact, whether he was traded to the 49ers or to whichever team can acquire him.

Potential landing spots: Vikings, Seahawks

The Raiders have reportedly not received any calls about Cousins, nor are they interested in trading him. I wouldn't be surprised if that changed, however, with teams at least checking in on his availability before Tuesday's deadline. Las Vegas has Fernando Mendoza, the No. 1 overall pick at the 2026 NFL Draft, waiting in the wings. The club has been diligent in his development, but they'll have to turn the keys over to him at some point. If they believe that he's ready, it makes sense to ship out Cousins for future assets. If they do come to that realization, Cousins landing with a team like the Vikings -- whom he played for from 2018 to 2023 -- it'd flip the NFC North on its head. He'd be an upgrade over Kyler Murray -- who is dealing with a Grade 2 hamstring injury -- and complement the best defense in the NFL. Minnesota would be taken even more seriously as a Super Bowl threat.

With Zach Hyman and Ryan Nugent-Hopkins out of the lineup, the Oilers haven't missed a beat thanks to its trio of superstars.

#2677. Confirmed lineups: 1. FC Köln vs Bayer Leverkusen

Draymond Green made it to November (barely) before earning his first ejection of the 2026-27 NBA season.

On Monday night, Green took exception to getting knocked over by Phoenix Suns center Khaman Maluach posting up in transition and got up and tackled Maluach, wrapping him up with both arms and throwing him to the ground -- Maluach still made a basket for an and-1. Draymond Green was assessed a double technical on this play and was ejected. pic.twitter.com/uCmsTQxmcX

The ejection is Green's 31st of his career and he now has three technical fouls this season, tied for the most in the league. Once a player reaches 16 technicals in a season, it triggers an automatic one-game suspension.

Without Green, the Warriors surged back from a double-digit second-half deficit to get a 116-113 win thanks to Stephen Curry's heroics with 34 points and a huge game off the bench from Charles Bassey, who scored 19 points and pulled down eight rebounds in 22 minutes due to Green's absence.

Bassey's 19 points in 22 minutes off the bench on Monday night equals Green's 19 points in 159 minutes of play this season. Green does lead the Warriors in assists (6.3 per game), and the offense hums around him with Curry and rookie star Yaxel Lendeborg combining for more than 50 points per game.

With the win, Golden State improved to 5-3 on the season and now sits in seventh in the Western Conference standings early in the season as the Warriors try to claw their way back to the playoffs for the first time in three seasons.

When the Cleveland Browns announced that Shedeur Sanders would be starting Sunday's matchup against the New Orleans Saints, no one was sure what to expect. Deshaun Watson was not exactly the fan favorite to win Cleveland's quarterback battle this offseason, but he led the Browns to a 5-3 start with five game-winning drives. After Watson suffered a concussion during the Week 8 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers, it was Sanders' turn to show what he could do.

The second-year signal-caller completed 19 of 31 passes for 297 yards and two touchdowns in a 23-22 overtime loss in New Orleans. Sanders became the only quarterback to register multiple 60-yard completions this season, and the first Browns quarterback to throw for 250 yards, two touchdowns and zero interceptions in a game since Jameis Winston in 2024, per CBS Sports Research.

This was a bizarre yet entertaining affair that featured 33 total points scored in the fourth quarter and overtime after the final stanza began tied 6-6. Sanders himself also put together a sleepy performance through three quarters before the points started coming in bunches.

With Sanders in the lineup, we got to see how he operates with all of Cleveland's new young talent. That includes Denzel Boston, who leads all rookie receivers in yards. He caught six passes for a career-high 98 yards on Sunday.

DENZEL BOSTON MOSSED HIM pic.twitter.com/ZZdzSZtnpj

After the Saints acquired a 9-6 lead in the fourth quarter, Sanders threw KC Concepcion's first NFL touchdown — a 64-yard pass where the versatile playmaker did most of the work. Concepcion caught four passes for 85 yards. He and Boston became the only rookie duo in the past 35 years to record 60-yard receptions in the same game.

KC FIRST TOUCHDOWN ON A 64 YARD PLAY#CLEvsNO on CBS pic.twitter.com/p4CPhjtQPA

Sanders also led a game-tying drive at the end of the fourth quarter. Down 16-13, Sanders took the Browns offense 41 yards down the field on seven plays to set up an Andre Szmyt 51-yard field goal. That includes this gritty throw to Jerry Jeudy for a gain of 30, where Sanders stood tall and delivered a strike despite taking physical punishment from Chase Young.

atta boy Jerry!!#CLEvsNO on CBS pic.twitter.com/Rwn09mqTZb

The Saints got the ball first to start overtime, and Tyler Shough marched his offense 74 yards down the field on 11 plays and found Juwan Johnson for a touchdown. When Sanders took over, he threw a 39-yard touchdown to Harold Fannin Jr. that will go down as one of the plays of the year.

There was no crowd-caused earthquake, but it was reminiscent of Marshawn Lynch's run against the Saints in 2011.

39 YARD TD FOR THE YAC KING HAROLD FANNIN!#CLEvsNO on CBS pic.twitter.com/EwW2lYo1UA

Todd Monken elected to go for the win instead of the tie and sent his offense out for the two-point conversion. Unfortunately, Sanders' pass to Boston fell incomplete, and the Browns fell to 5-4.

Game over in New Orleans. pic.twitter.com/e4pTvX7Ao4

It was a pretty good game from the Browns' QB2, but was it good enough to get him promoted to QB1? CBS Sports analyst and Steelers legend Bill Cowher thinks so.

"Shedeur Sanders should be the starter for this football team. He's going to be the future, and I think what he showed today — his resilience — he continued to come back, he made great decisions, he extended plays. I love the way he played and I would move forward with Shedeur Sanders," Cowher said.

"Shedeur Sanders should be the starter for this football team. He's gonna be the future."@CowherCBS loved what he saw from the @Browns young QB despite their loss 🔥 pic.twitter.com/elZ06pscOd

This performance would be good enough for Sanders to be promoted if Watson were disappointing. Again, Watson just became the third quarterback since 1970 to register a game-winning drive in each of a team's first five wins of a season. He's playing the best football of his Cleveland career. However, he's coming off back-to-back games with 300 passing yards, but also zero touchdowns.

Monken will surely be asked multiple times about his starting quarterback moving forward in the coming days, but right now, he's just proud that his QB2 stepped up and answered the bell.

"I'm really proud of him and how hard he's worked since I've been here," Monken told reporters. "He wasn't perfect. I wasn't perfect. But for a guy that really hasn't taken snaps with the ones in 10 weeks ... to come in there and continue to battle. Really, really proud of him. He's really matured."

#2671. MLB CBA negotiations timeline: League proposes delaying salary cap for 'smoother transition'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement.

The collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a new CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

To keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a new CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the important and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

To allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system."

MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It says it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.

In its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.

If labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June.

A poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN showed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt:

How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.

NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.

NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.

NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.

NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.

AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.

AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.

That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection.

MLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more quickly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:

All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.

During a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are:

Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus plan and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits."

The timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.

Commissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred says, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for."

"The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer says of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance issues in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse."

The MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include:

The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most issues are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward.

More face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:

MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league issues a statement that reads in full:

"The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50.

"Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a new 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players.

"We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans."

"After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their plan would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another.

"The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits.

"Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing new, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations."

Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system.

During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets.

MLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:

"Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB says in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans."

As for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.

The MLBPA also issues a statement in response to MLB's proposals:

Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:

Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.

U.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump says. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago.

"It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he said, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it."

Speaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred says. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed.

"We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us."

In a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer says. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

"Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars."

Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion."

"Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table."

MLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose:

Using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions.

On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap.

Another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries.

The MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:

"Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer says in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide."

"We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin says in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll."

Negotiations on a new CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key issues to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.

The 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a new agreement.

#2670. NFL Week 9 winners and losers: Ja'Marr Chase, Packers WRs go ballistic while Drake Maye's turnover woes return

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Ja'Marr Chase has been in the top tier of NFL wide receivers since he entered the league with the Bengals in 2021 and proved on Sunday why he belongs in the superstar echelon. Week 9 brought the absolute best version of the three-time All-Pro. He showed off his pass-catching prowess to an international audience with the best first half of his career in the 2026 Madrid Game.

Back on American soil were a number of other star-caliber performances but also a handful of lowlights. The Washington Commanders were among those teams who left something to be desired when they fell to 2-5-1 on the year, and on an individual level, Drake Maye turned in a dreadful performance and tossed three interceptions for the second time this season.

For every standout showing, there is typically an inverse effort that is equally as poor. Here are the biggest winners and losers from Sunday's Week 9 action across the NFL.

The final box score shows that Chase had himself a massive day in Madrid. The Bengals receiver caught 10 passes for 155 yards and a touchdown in the 34-17 win over the Atlanta Falcons and was integral in his franchise securing its first win on international soil. Far more impressive than his totals, however, was the percentage of that production that came in the first half alone.

Chase hauled in eight of his receptions in the game's first half hour. The touchdown and 142 of his yards also came in the opening half. The yardage was the most in any first half of Chase's tremendous career and the most in a first half by a Bengals wide receiver since 1988.

In the process, Chase joined Randy Moss as the only two wide receivers in NFL history with at least seven touchdowns in each of their first six seasons.

There is a three-man tie for the most turnovers in football, and Drake Maye joined that group on the heels of a disastrous showing in the Patriots' defeat. His 13 turnovers match those of Daniel Jones and Justin Herbert, who own the two lowest passer ratings in the NFL. His season-long tally ballooned with three interceptions against the Packers, and it hardly took any time for him to put one in the ledger, as the first pick came in the game's opening minute.

Maye settled in following a brutal start to the year and had only tossed one interception in his last four games heading into Week 9. But he reverted back to the tendencies that made him a major disappointment in September, and the Patriots suffered because of it.

The Green Bay Packers might just have two star wide receivers. It helps to have a red-hot quarterback in Jordan Love throwing to them, but Christian Watson and Matthew Golden have both taken sizable steps forward this season and reached a new and historic level as a tandem in the 45-27 rout of the New England Patriots. They combined for 17 catches, 335 receiving yards and two touchdowns and became the first pair of Packers teammates with 150 yards and a touchdown apiece in the same game since 1942. They are also the fourth duo in the NFL since 2020 with 160 yards and a touchdown each.

Most of Golden's work came in the first quarter. He was remarkable in the opening quarter with six grabs for 126 yards and his touchdown.

This receiving group is among the reasons why the Packers are in play for the hotly contested NFC North title, and the passing game looks capable of going toe-to-toe with any in the league. That could pay dividends in the postseason.

The same team that botched a last-second situation earlier in the year and thus settled for a tie instead of a potential win delivered another head-scratcher a few weeks later. The Commanders needed a touchdown to force overtime or take the lead against the Rams and had mere seconds to obtain it when they made two questionable calls.

With eight seconds to play in a 20-13 game, quarterback Jayden Daniels took a deep shot and left the ball short of the goal line. That would have been a reasonable throw if the Commanders had any timeouts at their disposal, but they were out of them at that point of the fourth quarter. A completion in that spot would have ended the game. Then, on the final play of the afternoon, Washington dialed up a hook-and-ladder play instead of a Hail Mary, which came up well shy of the end zone. Rather than having Daniels chuck the ball 31 yards, they looked for something underneath that was not there.

Coach Dan Quinn and offensive coordinator David Blough have drawn significant scrutiny, and those end-of-game decisions will not pull them out from under the microscope.

It took until Week 9, but the Los Angeles Rams were finally able to unleash a ridiculously talented defensive line duo of Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald. Garrett made his first appearance since Week 1 as he returned from injured reserve and completed his comeback from an in-season knee surgery. It was his first game with Donald, who joined the lineup in Week 2.

Garrett said in advance of the 20-13 win over the Commanders that opposing offensive lines would have to pick their poison when dealing with the one-two punch of future Hall of Famers and that they would have fun exploiting any one-on-one matchups that came their way. He did just that when he racked up three sacks and a forced fumble in his first game back. It was his eighth career three-sack performance.

If Sunday was the last time Kirk Cousins suited up in a Las Vegas Raiders uniform, it would be a sour ending to his brief tenure with the franchise. Although the team reportedly wants to keep him, Cousins' name has been thrown around in trade discussions ahead of Tuesday's deadline. Perhaps the combination of the Raiders' unwillingness to move him and his turnover issues in a 38-17 loss to the San Francisco 49ers will keep him in town, though.

Cousins threw three interceptions and is now tied for the most three-pick games in the NFL since 2020. Only Tua Tagovailoa has as many such outings.

It would be a steep drop for Cousins to go from a potential trade piece and starter for a contending team to a second-string quarterback, but if the offense flounders in the weeks to come and the Raiders slip out of the postseason hunt, coach Klint Kubiak could hand the keys to the offense to Fernando Mendoza. The No. 1 overall pick will likely get a look as the starter before the season is done. Any further struggles from Cousins may expedite that.

Shedeur Sanders' terrific individual effort came with the caveat that it did not result in a win. The Cleveland Browns quarterback showed the makings of a viable starter in the 23-22 overtime loss to the New Orleans Saints, though. That is a development that gives the Browns some flexibility moving forward if Deshaun Watson falters upon his return from the concussion protocol. And it could even lead to an internal quarterback controversy if any of the Browns decision-makers view Sanders' 297-yard, two-touchdown performance as a successful audition for the job.

Even in defeat, Sanders came through in the clutch for the Browns. According to Next Gen Stats, the second-year quarterback was 4-for-12 for 141 yards and two touchdowns when under pressure in the second half and overtime. In his final three drives, Sanders connected with rookie wide receiver KC Concepcion for a 64-yard go-ahead touchdown pass with 5:21 to play, moved the ball into field goal range to send the game to overtime and threw a touchdown pass to Harold Fannin Jr. at the end of overtime. That 39-yarder to the tight end would have been a game-winner if the Browns pulled off the 2-point conversion.

A pair of division title contenders watched their lives flash before their eyes. Two quarterback injuries ended up being much less severe than they appeared in the moment, and that gave the Chiefs and New York Giants a sigh of relief, because they looked bad. Patrick Mahomes did not miss a single snap despite sustaining an arm injury, while J.J. McCarthy returned to his game after less than a quarter's worth of evaluation on the sideline and in the locker room with a hip issue.

Mahomes took a heavy hit to his throwing arm from Jets standout rookie David Bailey and coughed up the ball for a strip sack. He gripped his  throwing arm as he ran to the sideline in immense discomfort, but he was back out with the offense on their next drive and led the unit to a 21-0 second half shutout in a 23-point win.

McCarthy missed nearly the entire third quarter of the Giants' 19-11 win over the Philadelphia Eagles, and it was Jameis Winston who led a go-ahead touchdown drive in his absence. But he bounced back from a hard hit to his hip and kept the lead intact during the final period. In just his second start with the team since his arrival via trade, he guided the Giants to their first win in Philadelphia in 13 years and kept them in first place in the NFC East.

It was another disaster of a week for the Los Angeles Chargers, but at least they scored a touchdown. In fact, they scored two. The most woeful offense in the NFL had gone 12 quarters (tied for the longest drought in franchise history) and 37 possessions (the most since the 2023-24 Chargers) without a trip to the end zone until Justin Herbert connected with Quentin Johnston on an explosive 58-yarder.

That strike was far too little and far too late to avert another loss, though. The Chargers are still the only winless team in the league and are now 0-8 following their 44-22 defeat at the hands of the Houston Texans.

For the second time in his career, C.J. Stroud racked up at least 350 yards and five touchdowns in a game. He is the only player in Texans history to have done so twice. The breakout quarterback finished the day with 384 yards in the drubbing of the Chargers, which keeps him firmly on pace to outperform the career-best production he posted in his Pro Bowl-caliber rookie season in 2023.

Stroud was the NFL's passing yards per game leader in his debut season, and he also paced the league in interception rate. Following two underwhelming campaigns, he is back in that same form and could contend for the No. 1 spot on the leaderboard in both categories again. Houston's 3-5 record overshadows some of his individual success, but if he keeps playing like this, the Texans will have a chance to pull themselves out of a deep hole and compete for a spot in the playoffs.

It takes some luck to win one-score games in the NFL, but good teams create their own luck. The Denver Broncos are a good team. Their 26-21 win over the Carolina Panthers extended their winning streak in one-possession regular-season games to 16, which is the longest such streak in NFL history. The last time they fell short in one of those tight situations was all the way back in Week 3 of the 2025 season.

This one nearly got away from them, actually. The Broncos built a 26-14 lead with 5:41 to play but surrendered a touchdown and watched as the Panthers advanced to the 36-yard line in the final two minutes. A strip sack ended Carolina's rally and made edge rusher Nik Bonnitto the latest standout to play the hero role in this stretch of clutch wins.

All but one of Denver's seven wins this year have come by seven points or fewer. Doubters will argue that this is an unsustainable way to win, but Sean Payton's team just keeps pulling it off.

The silver lining for the Kansas City Chiefs is that their kicking woes did not haunt them in their three-score win over the New York Jets. But with the way things have gone on special teams this season -- and even dating back to last year -- one has to wonder how long Harrison Butker will keep his job. His persistent struggles are bound to cost the Chiefs in close games during the second half of the season and into the playoffs unless he turns a corner or the team removes him in favor of a more consistent field goal kicker.

Butker missed a field goal attempt at the end of the first half, but an offsides penalty negated the failed kick. He then missed the second try from five yards closer.

Only eight games into the season, Butker has already missed more attempts this year (seven) than in any single season during his career. He has now also missed 17 field goal tries since the start of the 2025 campaign. His miscues led the Chiefs to add Justin Tucker to their practice squad last month. It may be a matter of time before the team elevates Tucker to the active roster and ends the Butker era.

No team ever wants its punter on the field, but three squads made the most of fourth-down situations on Sunday. The Miami Dolphins and Detroit Lions turned their punters into offensive threats with a fake punt apiece, and in doing so, their matchup became the first game in NFL history wherein both teams' punters completed a pass.

Jack Fox of the Lions was the first of the two to successfully pick up a first down through the air. From his own 29-yard line, he threw a strike to Tay Martin for 11 yards and a new set of downs. Fox is now 5-of-6 passing for his career with 72 yards, and each of his completions resulted in a first down. The Dolphins pulled off a trick of their own in the fourth quarter when Bradley Pinon floated a ball to a wide-open Kaytron Allen, who rattled off a 46-yard gain on fourth-and-3 from Miami's own 36.

What a throw, @MrJackFox pic.twitter.com/n3m4I5phod

Dolphins draw up a fake punt of their own! That's two fake punts this game.DETvsMIA on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/caEvejdds1

Even regularly designed punts turned into highlights this week. Although Braden Mann was also responsible for a -2-yard punt, he flipped field position in the Eagles' favor with an 86-yard punt, which was the longest in the NFL since 2001 and the 10th-longest in franchise history.

#2669. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2668. NBA Bracketology: Projecting the full 20-team postseason field as Knicks, Thunder take steps back

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA comes at you fast. One moment the Knicks are riding high off their first championship in 53 years, the next they're off to a sluggish start and scrambling to recover from losing their first three games. The Thunder went into the season rightly hailed as one of the deepest teams in the NBA — then had that assumption tested in harsh fashion after sustaining injuries to three of their five starters, with Jalen Williams (ankle and fibula) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) expected to miss most, if not all, of the season, and Chet Holmgren (knee) out at least two months.

While OKC suffered the most brutal blows on the injury front, the Thunder are hardly alone there. Several big name stars have already gone down and missed multiple games, among them Anthony Edwards (knee), Kawhi Leonard (knee), Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring), Jalen Duren (hamstring), Paolo Banchero (ankle), Jaren Jackson Jr (knee) and Ja Morant (hamstring).

The net effect is that an NBA season that was already expected to be competitive and wide open — particularly in the East, where the conference is as deep as it's been in recent memory — has been thrown into flux. While the Spurs and Thunder remain the betting favorites to win it all, the Sixers, Knicks, Celtics, Rockets, Raptors and Timberwolves are bunched up right behind them, with the Nuggets, Pistons, Cavaliers, Lakers and Blazers not far behind.

In the actual standings, the new-look Sixers have won seven of their first eight and are perched atop the Eastern Conference, while the surprising Memphis Grizzlies got out to a hot start in the West and were the last team in the league to lose their first game after getting upended by the Pelicans in overtime at home on Monday night. Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Heat are under .500 and still trying to figure it out, while the Wolves and Warriors are just two teams out of several trying to stay afloat until key members of their respective teams return to the floor.

Various prediction models have differing opinions on what all this means in the long run. Those forecasts vary wildly, with one favoring the Raptors to come out of the East and another giving four other teams a better shot to win the conference than Toronto.

Predicting how all this will shake out in the end is difficult at best and folly at worst — so naturally that's exactly what we'll try to do over the course of the season.

This is our first installment of semi-regular NBA seeding predictions -- the NBA version of Bracketology -- where we'll give our best guess on where teams will be slotted once the playoffs roll around. The methodology is super scientific: watch a lot of basketball, consult with the mountain of stats and data available, and then eyeball it. Your mileage may vary.

Despite Duren playing all of 38 minutes this season, the Pistons have reminded everyone why they were the top seed in the East last season and have designs on something similar again this year. Detroit has proven to be a quality regular-season team, but the Pistons are still in desperate need of more shot creators and scoring to help ease the burden on Cade Cunningham. Their front office has work to do to level up the roster and avoid another disappointing postseason.

After what could charitably be called a tumultuous offseason, the Celtics once again look like a competitive, competent organization (apart from their struggles in Houston on Monday in the second night of a back-to-back) that figures to be a tough out in the East. Jayson Tatum is playing well enough to openly wonder "why not me?" when it comes to the MVP conversation, while Paul George's numbers to start the season look a lot more like the PG we saw in his final campaign with the Clippers rather than (mercifully for him and Boston) the lackluster version who was only intermittently available during his time in Philadelphia.

There were questions about the new-look Sixers going into the season, mainly how four big-name stars in the starting lineup would co-exist. The answer to date is that they've figured out ways to win when things have sometimes looked bleak. The Sixers lead the league in clutch victories, with six of their seven wins coming in games decided by five points or fewer with under five minutes to go. More surprising: they're top five in defensive rating and have allowed the second fewest points per game.

On paper, the Knicks have the best starting five in the NBA. That hasn't changed. Even though they didn't start the season looking like the dominant version of themselves that ripped through the playoffs en route to a title, the talent in New York remains undeniable.

The Raptors were a good defensive team last year and figure to be so again, but how far Toronto goes this season will be directly tied to Kawhi's availability — something that has been largely unknowable for much of the last decade of Leonard's career. As for the Cavaliers, their starting five is among the best in the league. After that, the roster gets thin and the questions begin to mount for Kenny Atkinson and the analytics team.

Maybe this is disrespecting the Hawks by lumping them with three teams that hardly inspire confidence, but the East feels like it has a solid six and then a pretty squishy bunch jockeying for play-in positioning. Miami fans won't like being in this group either — even though members of the Heat overreacted to their ugly start just like the rest of us and wondered aloud about the floor spacing and fit between Giannis and Bam Adebayo. Banchero is once again hurt in Orlando, but even when he's healthy, he and Franz Wagner (who is still searching for his elusive 3-point shot) have achieved exactly nothing together. The Wizards have been surprisingly plucky to begin the season, but if you're skeptical about Trae Young and Anthony Davis being on the floor enough to actually influence their record and help them sneak into the play-in, you aren't alone. Feel free to swap out the Hornets for one of these last-chance slots; Charlotte has been without the services of Kon Knueppel (hamstring) thus far and would undoubtedly benefit from his return.

Not pictured: the Pacers, who will be going nowhere fast if Haliburton and Ivica Zubac (ankle) don't get back on the floor sooner than later and stay there.

The Spurs are the biggest beneficiaries of the league-wide injury virus that has yet to infect them. The defending Western Conference champs are healthy, which is more than most teams can say. They still need to figure out the crowded and sometimes clunky backcourt fit between De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper, but as long as Victor Wembanyama is available, the West is once again theirs for the taking.

The Rockets were sorely in need of guard play last season after Fred VanVleet missed the season with a knee injury. He's back, and Houston has looked stout at both ends of the floor to begin the season (including Monday evening's comfortable home win over the Celtics). But is FVV's return enough to boost the Rockets and propel them to a deep postseason run, or does Houston need to make a move in a conference that is suddenly up for grabs outside of San Antonio? There will be endless rumors between now and the trade deadline about how the Rockets could use someone like Kyrie Irving — which does not mean the Mavericks will be keen on moving him.

If there's any team that could withstand losing three of its five starters for a significant chunk of the season, it's OKC. Sam Presti has done a masterful job making the Thunder into the deepest team in the league, but this represents the biggest challenge OKC has faced since developing into a perennial contender. How much weight can Shai Gilgeous-Alexander be reasonably expected to carry, and will guys like Ajay Mitchell, Isaiah Hartenstein, Alex Caruso, Jared McCain, and rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz be able to fill the void created in the absence of Williams, Wallace and Holmgren?

Luka Dončić is off to a scorching start, leads the league in scoring and has played better defense at times (and doesn't mind saying so himself), though even JJ Redick has openly questioned the roster and what the ancillary parts can be reasonably trusted with on a nightly basis. The Nuggets are once again thin after the starting five and are heavily reliant on Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray. And through the first five games, the Blazers boasted the third-best point differential in the league — but also lost Morant to a hamstring injury that will keep him out of the lineup for a while. At least it's Dame Time in Portland again.

There were those of us who doubted the fit with Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball and wondered whether the duo could make the Wolves into contenders — and that was before the team announced that Edwards would undergo an unexpected in-season knee surgery. That's asking Ball to do a lot in his absence. Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has played well and talked even better, but Golden State is still painfully thin while waiting for Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody to return from knee injuries (to say nothing of Kristaps Porzingis, whose status remains a mystery). Kyrie's name has been unsurprisingly floated in various trade rumors, but the Mavericks just might be competitive enough to entertain keeping him around. After moving on from Desmond Bane, Jaren Jackson Jr and Morant, the Grizzlies were supposed to be rebooting the franchise around rookie Cam Boozer. Memphis benefited mightily from a paper-thin schedule to start with wins over the Jazz (twice), Kings (twice), Warriors and Blazers before the Pelicans finally handed them their first L. It only gets harder from here — but even qualifying for the play-in would represent a successful season in Memphis.

#2667. MLB proposes delaying salary cap in new negotiations as Dec. 1 CBA expiration inches nearer

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball has proposed delaying the implementation of a salary cap/floor system until 2028 as part of its latest collective bargaining agreement proposal, the league announced Tuesday. MLB says the delay is intended to provide a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system and give teams more time to prepare and get their payrolls in order.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system without delaying key player benefits, including earlier free agency, a $1 million minimum salary, a 30% increase to the pre-arbitration bonus pool, and transactional reform that will reduce roster churn."

The league also newly proposed a $180.2 million salary floor and a $258.2 million salary cap. Those numbers are up from $171.2 million and $245.3 million, respectively, in the league's previous proposal in June. The $1 million minimum salary would only apply to players with at least two years of service time. The minimum salary would be $900,000 for all other players.

Four teams currently have more than $258.2 million on the books for 2027 (including arbitration projections) and 20 teams have less than $180.2 million on the books, according to FanGraphs' calculations. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027 before the transition to a salary cap/floor system in 2028.

The collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and the owners are expected to lock out the players at that time. The previous lockout ended on March 10, then there was a three-week spring training leading up to Opening Day. If there is a similarly lengthy lockout, it would be impossible for clubs to become salary cap-compliant in such a short period of time.

The MLB Players Association has repeatedly insisted it will not accept a salary cap/floor system, and has instead proposed a revised revenue sharing system that would funnel more money from big-market teams to small-market teams. In a statement following the league's proposal on Tuesday, the MLBPA accused owners of continuing to "propose blowing up the current system and replacing it with one designed to line their pockets and increase their franchise values." The union also said that even with a delayed implementation, the league's proposal of a salary cap maintains the same "negative impacts," including a "massive reduction in player compensation" and the "elimination of fundamental player rights, including guaranteed contracts."

MLB says its push for a salary cap/floor system is intended to improve competitive balance. The small-market Milwaukee Brewers defeated the small-market Tampa Bay Rays in the World Series last week and swept big-market teams (Los Angeles Dodgers and New York Yankees) en route to the Fall Classic.

#2665. SC Freiburg vs. Union Berlin preview: Freiburg look to continue title push against struggling Union

Ironically, the 640km separating Berlin and Freiburg im Breisgau is a pretty accurate representation of where the teams currently sit on the table: with a win, Freiburg can push their way back into 3rd place as they continue hunting for a UEFA Champions League spot and maintain their pressure on Dortmund and Bayern, while Union Berlin could potentially sink back down into the relegation zone depending on Schalke’s outcome.

Will we see a shock at the Europa-Park Stadion, or will we see the points gap between both sides continue to widen?

Let’s begin with the home side, SC Freiburg.

Freiburg have been on a burner to commence the 2026/27 season with 5 wins, 3 draws and a solitary loss only coming against champions Bayern München, along with a respectable +8GD (18 goals scored). In addition to this, Freiburg ensured their Pokal survival by staving off recently relegated Wolfsburg with a last-gasp winner by Keisuke Gotō. The team from Baden-Württemberg also had a healthy start to their Conference League campaign with 2 wins and 1 loss, their most recent result being a 1-0 away win against Trabzonspor.

To go back to the Bundesliga, Freiburg managed to overcome a 1-0 deficit to Augsburg to come away from Bavaria with a 2-1 win in their most recent match. A win against Union Berlin would see them not only move back up to 3rd, but also come to within 2 points of league leaders Borussia Dortmund and Bayern München.

Apart from their 3-1 loss to Bayern München, Freiburg have been otherwise flawless at home and look poised to strike while the iron’s hot as they push for a first-ever UCL qualification.

A duo to watch this match will certainly be the strike partnership of Igor Matanović and Yuito Suzuki, who account for 8 goals (4 goals each) - nearly half of Freiburg’s total goals this season.

SC Freiburg will be without Florent Muslija and Patrick Osterhage.

Ironically, the club known as “Eisern Union” (Iron Union) seem to have let their iron cool down as they sit near the bottom of the table as one of the league's most out of form teams.

Since shocking the footballing world by qualifying for the UCL in the 2022/23 season, Union Berlin has in fact looked quite malleable in recent seasons (I promise that’s the last metal-related joke I will make!), with this season shaping up to be a relegation survival battle for the Berliners.

With only 1 win in 8 games thus far (4D, 3L), Union squandered their previous Bundesliga matchup against 1. FC Köln at home, losing out on some much needed points with direct relegation rivals. This followed a 5-0 battering by that very same Köln team in the Pokal less than a week prior.

The bad news for Union continues if we look at their away form thus far - in just 3 matches, Union has drawn 1 and lost 2, with a shocking -11 goal differential (1 scored, 12 conceded), by far the worst in the league.

With local rivals Hertha Berlin having just beaten top-of-the-table rivals Wolfsburg and continuing their flawless run in the 2. Bundesliga (10W, 1D, and a +16 GD), the pressure is surely beginning to mount on Union securing their status as Berlin’s best team.

Union Berlin will miss the likes of Andrej Iic, Stanley Nsoki, Andrik Markgraf and Robert Skov. Felix Uduokhai remains out via suspension after his red card against Augsburg.

To give Union fans a bit of hope, Freiburg have had a shaky record in recent years against the team from Berlin.

Union have been flawless against Freiburg in their last 7 matches (4 wins, 3 draws, and outscoring Freiburg 9:4), with their last loss occurring nearly 4 years ago to the day. Union is also currently on a 2-game winning streak against Freiburg when playing in the Europa-Park Stadion.

This does come with a caveat however, which is that both sides were a lot closer in regards to form and table positioning in the same fixture last season - in 2025/26, Freiburg was 8th (34 points, -5 GD) while Union was 11th (28 points, -12 GD). This time, 16th place Union (7 points, -12 GD) will really have to punch up if they want to win against 4th place Freiburg (16 points, +8 GD).

If Union Berlin are to regain their form, perhaps they can make it happen against Freiburg and potentially eke out another win to pick up some much needed points and create some separation at the bottom of the table.
