#2634. Should the NBA shorten games to 40 minutes? Pros and cons of move as league battles early season injury crisis

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Opinions vary on the causes and potential solutions for the NBA's early-season injury crisis, and an idea commissioner Adam Silver once floated is back in the conversation. Sports Illustrated's Chris Mannix said on the Open Floor podcast that he has heard that Silver likes the idea of shortening NBA games to 40 minutes. This is an idea that Silver has previously supported publicly.

"As we get more involved in global basketball, the NBA is the only league that plays 48 minutes. And I would be -- I am -- a fan of four 10-minute quarters," Silver said on The Dan Patrick Show in 2025. "I'm not sure that many others are. Putting aside what it means for records and things like that, yeah, I think that a two-hour format for a game is more consistent with modern television habits."

Silver is not the only major supporter of the idea. Mark Cuban has vouched for it as well, and given the sheer number of notable injuries the NBA has endured so far this season, the league is suddenly in a position in which it probably needs to consider pretty drastic changes to keep its best players on the floor. Is the idea of a 40-minute NBA game feasible? What are the pros and cons here, and why do the negatives ultimately outweigh the positives? Let's dive in.

Some basic math: 82 48-minute games equals 3,936 minutes of regular-season basketball for every team, before overtime. Trim games to 40 minutes and teams instead play 3,280 regular-season minutes per year, or around 17% less total basketball. Fewer minutes means fewer opportunities for players to get hurt.

That much is essentially indisputable. Where things get more promising is in the theoretical, compounding effect of playing less. If players are likelier to get hurt when they're overworked, reducing their workloads could potentially limit those more vulnerable minutes late in games and seasons because they simply aren't accumulating the same degree of wear and tear.

Fresher players would hopefully be healthier players.

College basketball games are 40 minutes. WNBA games are 40 minutes. FIBA games are 40 minutes. The NBA is the outlier here. It is the only major basketball league in which games have those eight extra minutes, and standardizing games across the sport could make it easier to translate player production across leagues.

This isn't strictly a basketball phenomenon, either. Major League Baseball is in the middle of a renaissance sparked in part by game-shortening measures like the pitch clock. Silver acknowledged this in that Dan Patrick Show interview, calling a two-hour game "more consistent with modern television habits." It's simply easier to hold the attention span of a television audience for a 40-minute game than a 48-minute game.

This has certainly been less true in the "eight champions in eight years" era we are currently living through, but the NBA tends to be more predictable than other sports when it comes to playoff outcomes. The NFL's single-elimination format makes the best teams extremely vulnerable in the postseason, and baseball is so inherently volatile because pitcher performance makes upsets so common.

Over a seven-game sample, the better team usually wins out in an NBA playoff series. This isn't absolute, of course, especially with health and 3-point variance factored in, but Cinderella runs are relatively rare in basketball. Only two NBA champions were seeded lower than No. 3 in their conference, and neither came this century. Nearly twice as many No. 1 seeds (53) have won titles than all other seeds combined (27).

Smaller samples create more volatility. It's easier for an inferior team to overcome a superior one across 40 minutes than it is across 48. Every hot shooting stretch means more; every key player in foul trouble has to miss a larger portion of the game. If you view the NBA through a purely competitive lens, this is a negative. If you view the NBA primarily as an entertainment product, creating more upsets is a real benefit of shortening games.

NBA games may last 48 minutes, but nobody actually plays anywhere near that much anymore. In fact, nobody even averages 40 minutes per game anymore, with Jamal Murray leading the league at 38.4 minutes per game thus far this season. What this essentially means is that teams could largely maintain the workloads of their superstars in a 40-minute game and simply use their bench players less.

This is the immediate reason that a change like this isn't feasible. Why on Earth would the NBA Players Association go along with a change that trivializes the majority of its membership? Stars would suddenly be more valuable than ever because they'd be playing a greater proportion of the game, but everyone else becomes less valuable for the same reason.

This has enormous team-building implications as well. Suddenly, superteams would be back in vogue because tying all of your money and assets into two or three players would make more sense in a world where fewer players are needed to get through a game or season.

On this note, it's not even clear what sort of health benefits this change would actually create. Bench players would certainly stay healthier just for playing less... but would stars benefit from this at all? That's less clear, and the NBA is obviously far more invested in keeping the best players on the court than role players.

There are theoretical fixes here, but none are perfect. The NBA could put a minutes cap on individual players, but remember, stoppages aren't uniform. Say the league sets a 30-minute cap, and a player crosses that threshold because no timeout, foul or dead-ball turnover stops the game for him to leave. How does the league handle that? It could mandate that players sit one full quarter, but doing so would inevitably lead to star players essentially playing at least one full half.

There's no clean solution to this problem, and until someone finds one, it's hard to believe this sort of change is feasible.

The length of games is only a small component of what makes the NBA schedule so grueling. Shortening games to 40 minutes wouldn't eliminate the need to travel to 41 regular-season road games. It wouldn't remove back-to-backs from the slate either, and it wouldn't bake more time into the schedule for practice, conditioning or a longer training camp.

NBA basketball is simply more difficult to play today than it was in the past. Players are more skilled and athletic than they used to be, forcing them to cover more space, play faster and endure more punishment than they once did. Shortening the game wouldn't change how it is played.

That's the danger of any incremental solution. Shortening games would carry substantial costs to the NBA. Shorter games would mean fewer commercial breaks for the television product. If the league tries it and it doesn't work, it has sacrificed revenue for nothing and is therefore less likely to take bigger financial risks to reap more substantial rewards, such as cutting games from the schedule.

Even if records and statistics aren't that important in the grand scheme of things, they're treated as sacred components of league history by many fans. Even if every other major rule has been subject to change across eras, the length of the game has been stable. That makes comparing stats and records across history at least somewhat viable. That changes if you shorten the game. Modern records become nearly unbreakable.

If the league were willing to tamper with its history in this way, there are simply lower-risk changes it could make instead of shortening games. One concept: increasing the value of 3-pointers to four points and similarly pushing 2s up to three. Doing this would narrow the value gap between shots behind the arc and those inside it, thereby incentivizing players to take more mid-range shots and, theoretically, forcing defenders to cover less ground than they do currently. One reason a change like this is unlikely is that it would make comparing numbers across eras pointless.

The NBA may one day decide it's willing to break that glass, but it has given no indication that it is prepared to do so now.

#2632. MLB rumors: The only Oriole not on the trading block, Rays' Drew Rasmussen plan and Astros add to manager hunt

The Brewers have now been World Series champions for just one week (minus a few hours) and they should still be basking in the glory for quite a while. As the offseason marches on, the next big date will be Nov. 17, when decisions on qualifying offers are due from the eight players who received one.

In the meantime, the rumor mill should be ever-so-slowly churning. We'll round it up here.

The Houston Astros moved on from general manager Dana Brown in August and fired manager Joe Espada after the 2026 season. Newly hired general manager Randy Flores is now tasked with landing a new dugout boss, and a three-time MVP and future Hall of Famer is in the mix. The Astros will interview Albert Pujols for the manager job this week, per The Athletic.

Pujols has long made it known that he desires to be an MLB manager. He recently interviewed for vacancies with the Padres and Angels (both last offseason) and he also managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic this past spring. It should be further noted that Pujols is in the fourth year of a 10-year, $100 personal services contract with the Angels that was part of the mega-deal he signed with them as a player prior to the 2012 season as a player.

Other known candidates for the Astros manager job are Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta and Yankees bench coach (not to mention former Tigers and Angels manager) Brad Ausmus. Former Astros third baseman Morgan Ensberg, the manager of the Triple-A Rays affiliate Durham Bulls, will also interview this week, according to MLB.com.

The Orioles are willing to listen to trade offers on any player other than Pete Alonso as they seek both rotation and outfield help, according to The Baltimore Banner. The  Orioles reportedly aren't "actively shopping" any players, but they are looking for upgrades at starting pitcher and outfielder and realize one of the ways that could happen is via a trade.

Surely they wouldn't sell low on Gunnar Henderson, given his immense upside, so we can probably take him off the table unless some team makes it worth their while. There is a glut of infielders, though. With Alonso at first base and Henderson at short, they have Jackson Holliday, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Jordan Westburg and Coby Mayo for two spots. Even using one of the four at designated hitter, it's easy to see where a deal could happen.

Westburg and Encarnacion-Strand are under team control through 2029 while Holliday is controlled through 2030 and Mayo through 2031.

The American League champion Rays recently picked up the $20 million club option on All-Star starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen. That would be a franchise-record salary for one player in a single season. It might seem odd to exercise an option and then deal a player to an outsider, but locking Rasmussen in for a one-year deal makes him an attractive trade candidate instead of just letting him walk in free agency, and this is how the Rays generally operate. We've seen it so many times: they get ahead of losing guys to free agency, sometimes even dealing them a year or two earlier. They've done it with Randy Arozarena, Isaac Paredes, Tyler Glasnow and even going back to franchise legends like David Price, Evan Longoria and Ben Zobrist.

The Rays right now are saying they intend to keep Rasmussen for 2027.

"Not a declarative this, that, whatever, but I can sit here very confidently and say that every intention right now is thinking about Ras anchoring our rotation and how to make this team better going into next year," club president Erik Neander said on Tuesday, via the Tampa Bay Times.

If they want to contend again next year, it sure seems like they need Rasmussen, with Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta off to free agency. That leaves Rasmussen atop the rotation, followed by Shane McClanahan, Griffin Jax, Ryan Pepiot and a bunch of question marks. There are questions attached to McClanahan, Jax and Pepiot too.

#2630. Victor Wembanyama after historic 52-point, 24-rebound night: 'It should be more like this, more often'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Victor Wembanyama came into the 2026-27 season with expectations of taking over the title of Best in the World, but a dismal performance on opening night in a loss to the Thunder raised questions about whether we might see the Spurs' star plateau in his fourth year.

Those concerns were short-lived, as the Spurs have ripped off six straight wins after their 0-2 start. Wembanyama did his part on Wednesday night when he put together a historic stat line in a win over the Mavs, scoring 52 points, pulling down 24 rebounds and blocking eight shots in a 112-111 win.

CAREER NIGHT FOR VICTOR WEMBANYAMA 🚨🤯 52 PTS (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 24 REB (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 8 BLKFIRST PLAYER WITH 50+ PTS, 20+ REB, 5+ BLK SINCE BOB MCADOO IN 1974. pic.twitter.com/lHzUhYYSTz

It was a career-best performance for Wembanyama, who spoke after the game about finally starting to feel like he had his legs under him again after beginning the year battling an illness.

"I haven't been feeling great lately," Wembanyama said, via the Associated Press. "I've been sick for a while and today I felt like I got my legs back. So it should be more like this, more often."

While he's not going to average 52/24/8, an otherworldly stat line is what we've come to expect from the Frenchman, and he's starting to post those kinds of sensational performances more often. It's his third game in the last four with at least 36 points and his fourth game this season with five or more blocks.

For as great as he was against Dallas, Wembanyama still sees plenty of room for improvement. He highlighted his struggles shooting the ball, noting that it forces him to play a style that's less sustainable over the long haul of the regular season.

"I can still do more," Wembanyama said. "I mean, my shots weren't falling tonight and that forces me into a style of play that is exhausting. I can do it. I mean, the proof is here. I can do it, but I can be much better if my shots fall. I know it's just a matter of time."

Wembanyama has been pretty awful shooting the ball this season, hitting 24% of his threes and is just 11 of 36 from the mid-range this year. Perhaps getting his legs under him better and feeling more like himself can unlock his perimeter game, which would make him all the more terrifying.

That said, there's something encouraging for the Spurs about Wembanyama struggling to shoot and just finding a way to dominate anyway. One of the frustrations of watching the gigantic Frenchman is how he sometimes seems to forget he can basically get free buckets when he gets himself near the rim. While it's understandable that he'd want to conserve some energy in the regular season, noting it's "exhausting" to fight through defenders to get to the rim, it's what makes the Spurs the best version of themselves and that's going to be the mindset he needs in the postseason.

If he does get the jumper working, it'll lighten that load some and make the Spurs even more dynamic, but Wembanyama can't forget that his most dominant performances come when he's relentless in attacking the basket. If he can find the right balance, perhaps his proclamation that "it should be more like this, more often" can come true, and he can ascend to that Best in the World title as expected.

#2629. 2. Bundesliga: Bochum snatch dramatic late victory over Karlsruher SC

The hosts made an electric start and needed just six minutes to take the lead. Berkan Taz picked out Christian Rasmussen on the left-hand side of the penalty area, with the Danish forward taking aim and firing a superb effort into the far corner beyond Hans Christian Bernat.

However, Karlsruhe responded almost immediately. Just two minutes later, Marvin Wanitzek teed up Kevin Wiethaup on the edge of the penalty area, and the midfielder produced an equally impressive finish into the top corner to restore parity.

Bochum subsequently enjoyed more possession and looked the more threatening side, with Karol Mets going closest to restoring their advantage. The defender was unable to convert from close range after Philipp Hofmann had nodded the ball into his path, while Jarne Steuckers also tested Bernat with a powerful effort from outside the box.

Despite the hosts’ pressure, Karlsruhe remained organised and managed to keep the score level heading into the interval.

The visitors made a flying start to the second half and took the lead just five minutes after the restart. Following a Bochum corner, Shio Fukuda helped keep the ball alive before Tim Civeja spotted Timo Horn off his line and produced a sensational strike from around the halfway line, sending the ball over the goalkeeper and into the net to make it 2-1.

Bochum responded almost immediately, however, with Hofmann bringing the hosts level in the 53rd minute. After Taz delivered the ball into the penalty area, Rasmussen helped it into the path of the former Karlsruhe striker, who made no mistake from close range.

Both sides subsequently searched for a winner, with Bochum coming particularly close through Taz and Hofmann in the 74th minute. Bernat initially parried Taz’s effort before producing an outstanding reaction save to deny Hofmann from the rebound.

The Karlsruhe goalkeeper continued to frustrate the hosts as the game entered its closing stages, while Bochum also had to remain alert to the visitors’ counter-attacking threat.

However, Uwe Rösler’s side eventually found their breakthrough in the second minute of stoppage time. After Mansour Ouro-Tagba drove forward down the left, Hofmann helped the ball back into the path of Taz, whose effort was saved by Bernat. The resulting attack remained alive, and Karol Mets delivered the decisive ball into the penalty area for Hofmann to finish from close range and complete a remarkable comeback.

The late winner sparked celebrations around the Vonovia Ruhrstadion, with Bochum claiming all three points in an entertaining five-goal encounter.

The victory continues Bochum’s recent improvement under Rösler, while Karlsruhe will be left frustrated after twice taking the lead and ultimately coming away empty-handed.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2627. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

Here's how the preliminary lottery odds look for those 16 teams in the mix, based on how they finished the 2026 season:

It's too soon to know which players will be in the mix for that top pick since the amateur seasons haven't begun yet. However, two early favorites to go No. 1 are University of Florida shortstop Brendan Lawson and Mississippi State left-hander Tomas Valinicius.

#2626. Darius Acuff Jr. isn't a perfect rookie, but he may be just what the Kings need right now

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The usage rate leaders list through the first two and a half weeks of the NBA season features some familiar and expected names: Luka Dončić, Anthony Edwards (four games), Victor Wembanyama, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Stephen Curry round out the top five, with Brandon Miller and Jayson Tatum not far behind.

However, the name below them might come as a surprise. Kings rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr., who has a 31.6% usage rate through the first eight games, is No. 8 on the list.

The only other rookie in the top 40 is Bulls forward Caleb Wilson (No. 38).

Here are the last five players to win NBA Rookie of the Year, along with their respective usage rates.

Even with a sample size that represents barely 10% of the season, what Acuff is doing will likely be sustainable, as he's being asked to do more than any rookie in his class on the offensive end of the floor. It's for that reason that his play has drawn eyeballs and why everybody seems to have an opinion — whether it's positive, negative, or maybe even somewhere in between — on him.

Is the 19-year-old guard a perfect rookie? Absolutely not. But he is just eight games into his NBA career and is posting numbers that get him in the same conversation as players like Dončić, LeBron James and Oscar Robertson.

After finishing with 22 points and 12 assists in a loss to the Lakers on Wednesday, Acuff became the fastest NBA player in NBA history to reach at least 200 points and 50 assists. It's hard to imagine he won't be writing his name into the record books across his rookie season.

As someone who watched Acuff throughout his entire college career at Arkansas, I'm not surprised to see the numbers he is putting up in the NBA. Acuff was just the second SEC player (and the first since Pete Maravich) to average at least 22 points and six assists per game in a season.

John Calipari has coached plenty of outstanding one-and-done guards during his time at Memphis, Kentucky and Arkansas, including Gilgeous-Alexander, Devin Booker, Derrick Rose, De'Aaron Fox, Jamal Murray, John Wall, and Tyrese Maxey. Simply put: if you're an elite high school guard prospect, you want to play for Coach Cal.

Acuff's season at Arkansas had him in the conversation for the best freshman guard Calipari has coached. Does that mean he's going to become a two-time NBA MVP like SGA or a multi-time NBA All-Star like the other names on that list? The jury is still out, but his college production — on both ends of the floor — is similar to what we are seeing play out in the NBA.

For starters, Arkansas didn't have a deep roster, which meant Acuff was on the floor a lot. He played just over 35 minutes per game, which is slightly less than he's playing with Sacramento right now. The same depth issues Acuff experienced at Arkansas are what he's dealing with in the NBA with his new team.

The Kings don't have a true backup point guard, which means Acuff is playing more than anybody else on the roster. When Acuff comes off the floor, Sacramento has been playing Malik Monk as the de facto point guard — a role he has filled in spot minutes throughout his time with the Kings.

Ben Simmons was also expected to be in Sacramento's starting lineup this season, where he could've taken on some of the ball-handling duties in the first and second units, but he suffered a torn Achilles days before the 2026-27 season began. That leaves Acuff, most nights, to play the entire fourth quarter and run the offense with a team full of players who can't create their own shot.

While Acuff's offensive game is as good as anybody in his class, the knock on him during the pre-draft process was his defense. It showed up throughout his time at Arkansas, but in Acuff's defense (no pun intended), he was asked to be the primary engine of the offense while staying on the floor for most of the game.

In Sacramento, it's been more of the same.

Acuff isn't a strong defender, and projecting him as a net-neutral defender over the course of his career would be a big win for his development. The offensive end is where Acuff is going to make his money. His processing skills for his age are elite and will only get better.

Acuff to Sacramento was one of the worst-kept secrets throughout the entire pre-draft cycle. The connections between his family and Kings general manager Scott Perry run deep: Perry coached Darius Acuff Sr. when he played at Eastern Kentucky in the 1990s.

After Sacramento fell in the draft lottery and landed pick No. 7, it became almost too obvious that Acuff would end up a King. The Clippers coveted Keaton Wagler early in the cycle, while Brooklyn liked the shooting upside of Mikel Brown Jr. Even though the Kings were said to be deciding between Acuff and Kingston Flemings, the former felt inevitable if Acuff was indeed available when Sacramento was on the board.

With that context, it's easy to understand why he is being handed the keys to the offense immediately, despite being on a roster that includes former NBA All-Stars Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis. LaVine has the second-highest usage rate on the team (25.6%), while Sabonis — who thrived as the hub of Sacramento's offense during the 2022-23 season— has a usage rate of just 15.7%.

Even with a roster that might not look 1-7 bad on paper, the Kings simply don't have enough shot creation and shot-making outside of Acuff and LaVine. The stat that stands out? Only 23 of Acuff's 189 shots have been catch-and-shoot attempts, per Synergy. At Arkansas, Acuff thrived in the catch-and-shoot department, shooting 50% (60 of 120) in that category.

Please don’t try to hate on Acuff’s shot attempts if you don’t watch the Kings 😭Directing traffic for his own teammates, & they end up needing him to create a quality shot. He’s literally his entire team’s system. James Harden type shit. pic.twitter.com/ag5MWTcWAE

Acuff is averaging 23.6 shot attempts per game, which ranks second in the NBA, behind only Gilgeous-Alexander. While that stat might pop, most of the looks Acuff is getting have been a massive improvement from his NBA debut, where he shot 5 of 24 against the Clippers.

For a smaller guard, Acuff has done a great job of getting to the paint; he's shooting 25 of 52 (48.1%) at the rim. Acuff is also getting a healthy number of 3-point attempts. He shot 44% from beyond the arc at Arkansas, but has connected on just 30.8% of his 3-point attempts so far. Rookie guards are historically inefficient, so it shouldn't be that much of a cause for concern.

Sacramento seems to be waiting on the 2027 offseason to take a step toward a proper rebuild, though the front office has reportedly been trying to move LaVine and Sabonis — the two highest-paid players on the team — since Perry took over as GM in 2024. LaVine and De'Andre come off the books this summer, while Sabonis and Malik Monk (player option) are free agents in 2028.

The blueprint for building a team around Acuff — a player who can score at will and be the offensive engine for a team — should be what the Knicks have done with Jalen Brunson. New York surrounded Brunson with 3-and-D wings, which takes the pressure off him on the defensive end of the floor. Sacramento has just one true 3-and-D wing on the roster: Keegan Murray, who is currently out with an ankle injury.

With several high-priced veterans on the roster, this will be Sacramento's short-term future. The No. 1 priority this season for Sacramento is developing Acuff so when the big names come off the books and the team has cap space, the franchise can properly build a team around him.

One popular comparison Acuff has drawn, dating back to the pre-draft cycle, is Cam Thomas. No disrespect at all to Thomas — who was one of the best pure shotmakers and scorers in the league when he played — but Acuff is by far a more advanced passer and facilitator for his age.

Acuff is averaging seven assists per game, which ranks 12th in the league. He is also averaging 12.4 potential assists per game, per the NBA's tracking data, which ranks 11th. Acuff at Arkansas was an elite facilitator despite being a high-volume scorer. Over the last few games, Acuff has been making an effort to get his teammates involved in the high pick-and-roll.

This clip from Wednesday's loss to the Lakers is exactly the kind of play Acuff is making that won't show up on the box score: he falls over while making a cross-court pass to a wide-open shooter (Monk) who missed a 3-pointer. Acuff finished with 12 assists against the Lakers, but had 17 potential assists, per the tracking data.

Darius Acuff ter 7 assistências nesse jogo é um crime federal.O garoto tá fazendo tudo pra achar visuais para os companheiros de time e nada cai.Olha isso irmão… revoltante uma parada dessas. pic.twitter.com/TIu2m3Gm1X

Let's go back to Thomas, who didn't have a game with more than four assists during his rookie season. Acuff has recorded at least five assists in six of his first eight games, including two with over 12 assists.

Acuff's passing was one of his strengths throughout his college career. He is a very good lob passer who routinely made tough cross-court or skip passes with multiple defenders in the area. While Acuff is known for scoring, his passing is underrated.

Acuff isn't a perfect rookie, but he isn't even 20 years old and Sacramento projects as one of the worst teams in the NBA. The Kings will happily trade the good for the bad if he continues to develop and post the numbers he's putting up.

#2625. Patrick Mahomes injury update: MRI reveals no significant damage to Chiefs QB's elbow

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Late in the first half of their blowout victory over the New York Jets, the Kansas City Chiefs got a significant scare. Patrick Mahomes dropped back to pass on a second-and-4 play coming out of the two-minute warning, and as he attempted to throw the ball downfield, his arm was hit by Jets edge rusher David Bailey. His elbow bent awkwardly backward, and he left the field with his right arm hanging by his side.

Mahomes already underwent an MRI after the game and it did not reveal a significant injury, according to ESPN. He will be monitored for pain and swelling throughout the week.

Patrick Mahomes was holding his elbow after this hit pic.twitter.com/jyzMdNfkwR

Mahomes ultimately didn't have to miss a snap because the Jets recovered the fumble on the play, and by the time the Chiefs got the ball back, Mahomes had gotten his arm warm while throwing on the sideline. He returned to play the rest of the game and finished the day 23 of 31 for 242 yards and two touchdowns, each on passes to Kenneth Walker III.

Mahomes, later in his postgame interview, said he didn't feel like himself at first when he came back into the game after the scare, but that things gradually improved as he settled into the second half.

"I felt like out of the half, I wasn't throwing the ball the way I wanted to," he said. "As the game went on — and we continued to work through it and it kind of got warmed back up — I thought I started throwing the ball better towards the end of the second half. That will be important this week is kind of getting the swelling and the fluid out of it so I can be ready to go from the first snap next week."

Mahomes further noted that he felt just fine after the game, but that he would have to go through the usual process to get himself ready for the Chiefs' Week 10 game against the Atlanta Falcons.

"I feel good now," he said. "Obviously, you get the win and the adrenaline's pumping. I'm sure I'll be sore tomorrow, but we'll get right to it. We'll get to work on it, and we'll get ourselves ready to go. It's great to get the win now, now it's about getting ourselves ready for next week."

#2621. How Victor Wembanyama's improved shot diet is leading him to historic heights

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After Victor Wembanyama authored the worst shooting game of his career on opening night, a 1-for-13 showing in a loss to the Thunder, I wrote that the Spurs' honeymoon was over. It was dramatic by design -- a play on the early-season, and in this case single-game, overreactions we always get at the start of every new campaign.

But there was truth in it. Last year, everything the Spurs did was on house money. Winning 62 games. Eliminating the defending champion Thunder on the road in Game 7 of the conference finals. Holding the lead vs. the Knicks for 72% of total minutes played in the Finals. Wembanyama unanimously winning Defensive Player of the Year and finishing third in MVP voting. All prologue, no expectations.

This year, the real story starts, and we knew the benefit of the doubt would be gone. When Wembanyama laid that opening-night egg, the chatter started. He was crowned too soon. He doesn't have a go-to shot or spot. After that game, Wembanyama had no need for the critics. He was his own biggest critic, lamenting his hesitancy and overthinking, saying he needed to "go back to playing the basketball I like."

"I got no reason to be hesitant, no reason to not be myself," Wembanyama said. "For me, it's as simple as that. I'm good when I have fun."

Suffice it to say, he's been having plenty of fun since. Over his last seven games, Wembanyama is averaging 31.4 points, 12.2 rebounds and 4.3 blocks on 52% shooting. After opening 0-2, San Antonio has won six straight, with the latest being Wednesday night's 112-111 thriller over the Mavericks, who erased a 19-point deficit to tie the game with under two minutes to play.

In the end, Wembanyama was just too much. He scored the Spurs' final seven points and 11 of their last 13 and hit the game-winning free-throw. When it was all said and done, the box score read like something out of a video game: 52 points, 24 rebounds and eight blocks as he became the first player to hit those marks since Bob McAdoo more than a half century ago.

CAREER NIGHT FOR VICTOR WEMBANYAMA 🚨🤯 52 PTS (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 24 REB (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 8 BLKFIRST PLAYER WITH 50+ PTS, 20+ REB, 5+ BLK SINCE BOB MCADOO IN 1974. pic.twitter.com/lHzUhYYSTz

Actually, that's selling Wembanyama short. McAdoo only had seven blocks in that 1974 game against the Celtics. Filter it for at least 50, 20 and eight blocks, and only Wilt Chamberlain has done it, and that was before blocks became an official stat. The dude had 29, 15 and five in the first half, for crying out loud. No player in the last 30 years has registered that halftime line.

OK, so Wembanyama is a beast. We all knew this. He's going to have a lot of historic-number games. But what's interesting about the anatomy of this one is where the production came from on the floor, which has quietly been the story of his season.

Wembanyama's shot diet became one of the seminal stories of last year's postseason. He's a relatively random player on the offensive end, and there were stretches when his ability to dance on the perimeter and shoot from range was becoming too easy of a crutch. He's a fine shooter and has a capable handle; for his size, he's extraordinary. But when the listed 7-foot-4 guy who is probably closer to 7-foot-6 is camping out around the 3-point line, it's a win for the defense, particularly at scale.

We saw both sides of this dynamic throughout the playoffs as Wembanyama waffled between a perimeter- and paint-based structure almost from game to game. We saw it against Minnesota in the second round. We saw it again against Oklahoma City in the conference finals when Wembanyama dominated Game 1 at the rim only to be literally pushed out to the perimeter in the following games by Isaiah Hartenstein.

Over the first two games of the Finals, Wembanyama took more shots from outside the paint (22) than he did inside (20), a win for the Knicks, who went up 2-0. In Game 3, he flipped the script, taking 13 of his 18 shots from inside the paint as the Spurs won in a blowout.

There won't always be a direct correlation between Wembanyama's shot diet and the Spurs' outcomes; they're going to win most of their games on sheer talent, and Wembanyama is going to pile up massive numbers for the same reason. But the details matter at the highest level, and so far this season Wembanyama is operating closer to the hoop with greater intention.

Through these first eight games, Wembanyama is taking five more shots a night than he did last year. Nearly all of them are coming from inside the paint, as you can see in the table below highlighting his field-goal attempts from each area.

As a matter of percentage, Wembanyama is taking 42% of his shots from inside three feet this year, up from 33% last year. Those 5.1 dunks per game put him on pace for more than 400 this season, which would obliterate Rudy Gobert's NBA record of 302.

How is Wembanyama doing this? It's not a traditional thing where he's just posting up lower (which he isn't yet strong enough to do on demand and may not ever be), and there still isn't a specific spot or shot he is establishing as the go-to move everyone is clamoring for. It's just the intent to get down there, whether it's by rim rolls, crashing the offensive glass, or forgoing some of the settle 3-pointers for show-and-go drives.

Look at the clip below. He could've taken this initial 3, but he didn't. Instead, he got off the ball to establish himself 10 feet closer to the hoop, where he's now one cut away from a dunk as the Spurs have five 3-point threats on the floor who have collectively pulled every defender away from the basket.

Stephon Castle ⬆️ Victor Wembanyama 👽🤝🏰#NBAHighlights pic.twitter.com/NUX2JAQQ3G

That is what a concerted effort looks like. The seas may not always part like that, but Wembanyama is making it a point to occupy lower positioning more often, where he's ready and able to strike when the slightest crack presents itself. In many cases, Wembanyama is just hanging out beneath the basket or in the dunker's spot along the baseline from the start, rather than having to fight down there after he's started the possession 30 feet away.

One thing the Spurs are doing is initiating pick-and-rolls lower on the floor, so that Wembanyama, with his length, is a single turn from the front of the rim rather than having to navigate all the way from the 3-point line, which gives defenses time to clog his path.

HE'S GOT 47 PTS! 📺 ESPN, @DAZN, @CW35SA pic.twitter.com/ck0iYgngLs

This isn't rocket science. Wembanyama can go up so much higher than everyone else that it's simply a matter of him being near the rim. From there, the Spurs are just throwing it up as you would to an adult playing with kids.

Where Wemby catches the ball for this alley oop is ABSURD pic.twitter.com/azoeaeWUyv

Even the off-the-backboard lobs that Wembanyama is throwing to himself are more than a social media highlight. Note where he's catching the ball: at the free-throw line. When Wembanyama is one step from the rim, just about anything is at his disposal.

WEMBY IS SCARY 😧 pic.twitter.com/A4tPuDvQoa

De'Aaron Fox has talked about running these pick-and-rolls with Wembanyama where he's popping into the free-throw area for soft-spot jumpers, which are going to be there any time he wants as defenses sag back in an attempt, to whatever degree possible, to discourage dunks.

Those shots are about as close to a guaranteed clean look that Wembanyama can get from inside the arc. They are not going in at the moment. He's just 28% from 10-16 feet. But these are the stations from which he can play entirely on his terms. The 3-pointers, particularly the pull-up ones, are on the defense's terms, though he can make them and on plenty of nights will.

So far this year, Wembanyama is making just 24% of his 3s. That will go up, and the threat of him making that shot serves San Antonio's spacing well. He shouldn't, and won't, quit taking them. When they start going in, it could get flat-out unstoppable. But it's a fine balance, and Wembanyama is rightfully erring more on the lower side of the floor this year.

When Wembanyama scored his previous career high of 50 points in 2024, he did so on the strength of eight made 3s. On Wednesday, he only made one 3, while making 15 of his 20 shots from inside the arc. By aggressively going into the paint, he's also in position to draw more fouls, and indeed he made 19 free throws against the Mavs.

That is old-school center stuff. Just flat-out dominating inside. Wembanyama can obviously get buckets either way, but the closer-to-the-hoop way is the better bet all things being equal. On some level, this is pretty simple for a player this size, and you can see Wembanyama starting to figure that out.

#2620. Group of retired MLB umpires, including Joe West, file lawsuit alleging they are owed more than $2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former MLB umpire Joe West is part of a group of five retired umpires who are suing their pension plan and alleging they have been underpaid by the plan, the Associated Press reports. West, along with Tom Hallion, Gerry Davis, Larry Vanover, and Jerry Layne, filed the suit in late September in federal court in New York.

The suit alleges that the five umpires have been underpaid by the pension plan by more than $2 million. According to the AP, the suit "was filed against the American Leagues and National Leagues of Professional Baseball Clubs Retirement Income Plan for Umpires and that entity's retirement committee." The five umpires claim their benefits were not calculated correctly and therefore should receive additional money.

West, 74, retired from umpiring in MLB in 2021 after umpiring more than 5,000 games at the highest level starting in 1976. The man they called "Cowboy Joe" umpired a record 5,460 games in all, was known as a colorful figure in the sport and sometimes even a source of controversy.

In 2021, West won more than $500,000 in damages as the result of a defamation suit against former MLB player Paul Lo Duca after Lo Duca alleged during a podcast that West would "open up the strike zone" for reliever Billy Wagner in exchange for driving one of Wagner's vintage cars.

West referenced his "history with lawsuits" on Thursday. From the AP:

West said that when he brought up the issue to the retirement committee, he was offered a relatively small sum. West said MLB senior vice president and chief employment counsel Steven Gonzalez told him: "If you don't like the number, sue us."

"Does Steve Gonzalez not know my history with dealing with lawsuits?" West said.

Like West, Davis also retired after the 2021 season while Hallion umpired through the 2022 season and Layne and Vanover stepped away after the 2024 campaign. The five sued as individuals and did not involve the umpires' union, their lawyer, Paul B. Holmes, said, per the AP.

A pretrial conference in the case is scheduled for Dec. 11.

#2618. 2. Bundesliga: Heidenheim and Hannover share the points in four-goal thriller

The visitors made the brighter start and came close to opening the scoring inside the opening 15 minutes. Benjamin Källman did well to get in behind the Heidenheim defence before pulling the ball back for Husseyn Chakroun, who somehow missed the target with the goal at his mercy.

Hannover continued to look dangerous, with Marcel Hartel and Stefán Teitur Thórdarson also threatening, while Heidenheim struggled to create much of note in the opening stages.

Despite the visitors looking the more likely to score, it was Frank Schmidt’s side who broke the deadlock shortly before half-time. A long-range free-kick from Paul Hennrich caused problems inside the Hannover penalty area, with Jean Hugonet inadvertently diverting the ball into the path of Tim Siersleben, who reacted quickest to head home from close range in the 43rd minute.

Heidenheim therefore went into the interval with a somewhat fortunate 1-0 advantage, despite Hannover having created the better opportunities during the opening 45 minutes.

Sandro Wagner’s side came out with renewed purpose after the restart and were rewarded for their efforts in the 55th minute. Källman picked out Thórdarson on the edge of the penalty area, with the midfielder producing a precise first-time finish into the bottom-right corner to bring Hannover level.

The visitors continued to build momentum and completed the turnaround just eight minutes later. Marcel Hartel delivered a dangerous corner into the penalty area, where Hugonet rose highest to power a header beyond Thomas Dähne and put Hannover 2-1 ahead in the 63rd minute.

However, their advantage lasted less than three minutes. Heidenheim responded through a corner of their own, with substitute Christian Conteh delivering an inviting ball towards the near post for Budu Zivzivadze to glance a header into the net and restore parity at 2-2.

Both sides subsequently pushed for a winner in an increasingly open encounter. Hannover continued to threaten through Chakroun, while Heidenheim looked to take advantage of their attacking momentum following the equaliser.

Neither side could find a decisive breakthrough during the closing stages, however, with the points ultimately shared after an entertaining afternoon in Heidenheim.

The result extends Heidenheim’s winless run, while Hannover will take encouragement from their second-half response after coming from behind to take the lead, even if they were unable to hold on for all three points.

#2616. Ex-Guardians catcher Bo Naylor testifies in defense of Emmanuel Clase, Luis Ortiz in MLB pitch-rigging trial

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Cleveland Guardians catcher Bo Naylor on Thursday testified in federal court that he perceived nothing untoward about disputed pitches thrown by former All-Star closer Emmanuel Clase and his former Guardians teammate Luis Ortiz, ESPN reports.

Naylor, who played five seasons for the Guardians, appeared as a witness for the defense in the ongoing federal trial in which prosecutors allege that Clase and Ortiz rigged multiple pitches for the benefit of co-conspiring bettors. In Clase's case, he's alleged to have done so in 17 games across a two-year period beginning in May 2023. Naylor, now a member of the Milwaukee Brewers, was catcher for some of Clase's disputed appearances during that span, including seven of the 18 pitches he's alleged to have rigged.

Naylor, a defense witness, was shown video replays of some of the pitches the government alleges were predetermined by Clase or Ortiz as part of the scheme. Naylor was behind the plate for many of them and said they looked like common sliders outside the strike zone. He said the scouting reports on the hitters Ortiz faced during the two pitches in question indicated that sliders low and away would be a "weapon."

In November 2025, Clase and Ortiz were indicted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York. According to the Department of Justice, both pitchers "agreed in advance with their co-conspirators to throw specific types of pitches and speeds of pitches." The Department of Justice alleged that the pair made at least $450,000 by rigging outings and throwing specific pitches to benefit bettors who wagered on the outcomes of those pitches.

Both Clase and Ortiz pleaded not guilty to those charges in November of last year. Clase and Ortiz have been on administrative leave since late June 2025 while Major League Baseball investigates. MLB has the authority to discipline the pitchers regardless of how the criminal trial plays out.

The pair could face up to 65 years in prison if convicted on the charges of wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to influence sporting contests by bribery, and money laundering conspiracy.

#2615. Bronny James faces uncertain NBA future after Lakers assign him to G League

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Lakers assigned Bronny James and rookie Cameron Carr to the G League on Thursday, the team announced. James is no stranger to the Coachella Valley Lakers, having spent time with them across his first two seasons. Still, such an early G League assignment isn't exactly an encouraging start to his third NBA campaign.

James, the 22-year-old son of LeBron James, played for the Lakers in the playoffs last season out of desperation due injuries, but when the team has been closer to full strength, he has failed to earn more than spot minutes in his first two NBA seasons. He struggled mightily in the preseason this year, as he shot just 4 of 16 from the field. And while he has always been a defense-first player, his size -- 6-foot-2 and 210 pounds -- has limited his upside on that side of the floor.

"I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer with us, but I don't think he's played well in the four preseason games," Lakers coach JJ Redick said in October.

Despite those preseason struggles, James survived final cuts as the Lakers ultimately waived former No. 17 overall pick Dalton Knecht to get their roster down to 15 players. The move was relatively surprising considering their draft status. While both Knecht and James have fallen short of the team's hopes for them, Knecht was a former first-round pick who had at least held a consistent rotation role early in his rookie season. He fell off after a failed trade to the Charlotte Hornets, but teams typically like to give their own first-round picks as many opportunities as possible to succeed.

Knecht has since signed a two-way contract with the defending NBA champion New York Knicks. He appeared in his first game on Wednesday, a blowout win over the Chicago Bulls, and he notched 10 points in 16 minutes. By comparison, James has scored four points in 12 minutes spread across five appearances this season.

James was drafted in 2024 and became the first player in NBA history to share the court with his father. Now the elder James is a member of the Philadelphia 76ers, and both teams are doing well after their separation. The 76ers have the NBA's best record at 8-1, and the Lakers aren't far behind at 7-2. But with his father gone and the Lakers thriving in his absence, the younger James is in a somewhat precarious position moving forward. His name carries less weight with the organization than it once did, and a team with championship ambitions isn't going to be willing to wait on the development of a second-round pick forever.

James' contract is guaranteed through the end of this season, but not guaranteed afterward. If he doesn't show progress quickly, he could be a trade candidate at the deadline or simply not retained after the season.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. Skubal is expected to sign in November, before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, though a deal is not imminent. Talks are underway, however, and his market is moving.

Skubal is expected to sign a record contract at least in total value, and possibly in average annual value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract ever given out. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander's matching $43.3 million salaries with the Mets years ago set the record for the average annual value for a pitcher.

The Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, and Yankees are among the teams linked to Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports the New York Post. Unless MLB and the MLBPA unexpectedly avoid a lockout, Sato must sign before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Otherwise, he will return to the Hanshin Tigers for 2027.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. He has significant power but also swing-and-miss and defensive concerns at third base, similar to Munetaka Murakami a year ago. Murakami slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games as a rookie this season, providing proof of concept for Sato.

The Nationals have signed center fielder Jacob Young to a four-year extension, reports FanSided. The deal is worth $23 million and includes an $8 million club option for a fifth year. The extension buys out Young's three arbitration years and one free agent year, with a club option for a second free agent year. He's now under Washington's control through 2031.

Young, 27, has always been a superlative defender. He unlocked a new level on offense this season, particularly in the second half, when he hit .301 with a .385 on-base percentage. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.
